title: Australia's newest fast-bowling sensation tipped for big things from a young age
text:
While Mahli Beardman's record-setting demolition of England may have stunned the visitors, those who watched his development as a junior say it's no surprise.

On a day when fresh hostilities in the Sandpaper scandal dominated the headlines, the West Australian fast bowler's 6/24 skittled the visitors and gave Australian cricket a much-needed bit of good news.

But for West Pilbara Cricket Association secretary Christy Reed, Beardman's talent was always obvious.

Beardman (right) receives a representative cap while playing junior cricket in WA's Pilbara. (Supplied: Christy Reed)

While hailing from Cowaramup in WA's South West, the 21-year-old played his initial junior and representative cricket for Dampier in WA's Pilbara.

Initially spotted by scouts at a talent clinic in Karratha in 2017 as a 12-year-old, Beardman progressed quickly through the junior representative ranks, eventually landing at WA Premier Cricket Club Melville when he moved to Perth.

Ms Reed said he made an impression early.

"He was a tiny little kid, but his bowling was absolutely natural talent," she said.

Beardman (left) was identified early as a talented young bowler. (Supplied: Andrew Hayes)

"So fast for his size, and he absolutely loved his cricket.

" He would even go down to the senior team, Dampier Taverners, training and bully them in the nets. "

She hoped Beardman's success would show other talented junior cricketers across the Pilbara what could be achieved.

"For years it was really hard for kids to have a pathway through to that upper level, but I imagine this would get more kids interested in the sport," Ms Reed said.

"I couldn't be happier for him, his family and for Cricket Australia."

WA Cricket country area manager Andrew Hayes was working in the Pilbara around the same time Beardman and fellow Dampier quick Josh Vernon were making their way through the system.

"To take six wickets against our old foe on debut is an incredible achievement, and we couldn't be prouder," he said.

Mahli Beardman (back row, second from right) representing the West Pilbara at Junior Country Week. (Supplied: Christy Reed)

Hometown pride

The pride was echoed in Cowaramup, who are keen to embrace Beardman as a favourite son despite competing claims from nearby Dunsborough and Margaret River.

Loading...

Cowaramup Cricket Club stalwart and secretary Bob Biddulph coached a six-year-old Beardman before his family moved north.

"Unfortunately, he was only there for one year … but it was the start of his cricket journey, so we're very proud of him," he said.

"We're claiming it down at Cowaramup that's for sure; I think everyone associated with the cricket club is very proud of that."

Mahli Beardman walks off Perth Stadium after taking 6/24 on debut for Australia in ODI cricket. (ABC News: Sam Tomlin)

Mr Biddulph echoed the importance of seeing regional cricketers performing well at international level.

"It just goes to show that it doesn't matter where you are; if you start off and you enjoy the game and stick at it and keep practising, the sky is the limit," he said.

"We've got quite a few junior teams this year, so for them to actually see one of their own making it on the big stage is quite exciting."

Game two of the three-match ODI series is at Adelaide Oval on Sunday.

title: Cape Town inquiry spoke to all Aussie bowlers, ABC understands
text:
All four bowlers from the 2018 Cape Town Test spoke to investigators as part of the inquiry into ball tampering, the ABC understands, running counter to claims by former opening batter David Warner.

Warner wrote on social media that Cricket Australia's investigation — which saw him and Steve Smith banned for a year, and Cameron Bancroft rubbed out for nine months — was poorly handled and had a pre-determined outcome.

"As far as I am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation. If that's correct, then how can CA push the idea that the bowlers didn't know?" Warner wrote.

But sources connected to the bowling group said Nathan Lyon, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc were interviewed. The other front-line bowler from Cape Town, current Test captain Pat Cummins, said during a marathon press conference on Friday that he spoke to investigators.

Sources close to the bowlers said they all spoke to investigators. (Getty Images: Scott Barbour/Cricket Australia)

"They were all interviewed. [Warner's] comments are just not true," one source told the ABC.

The ABC also understands Tim Paine was interviewed as part of the investigation.

Cummins is sadly mistaken In his detailed 70-minute press conference, Pat Cummins said he hoped he could draw a line under the brewing Sandpapergate civil war. David Warner quickly proved that won't be happening.

After Cummins's press conference, Warner said Cummins had "thrown [Usman Khawaja] under the bus" by rejecting Khawaja's claims that more people were responsible for sandpaper entering the field of play than Warner, Bancroft and Smith.

"The way it was handled in the first place, it was hard for us to go back and give more evidence," Warner said on Fox Sports before Friday's ODI between Australia and England.

"I feel like it was a botched investigation. It was a quick one to get it over and done with. Some of the questions were quite challenging in the way it was being planted on us [Warner, Steve Smith and Cameron Bancroft] and we had to move on and just accept responsibility."

Usman Khawaja (right) said it wasn't fair for three players to bear all the responsibility for ball tampering. (Getty Images: Nick Potts/PA Images)

And Warner has doubled down on social media.

"It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning, ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose and now they want to maintain the false narrative that bowlers had no idea," he wrote.

"That stinks of a cover-up."

Cricket Australia said in response: "As we have stated previously, all players were given the opportunity to speak at the time of the initial investigation and have had the ability to come forward with new evidence in the eight years since.

"Subsequently, CA has respected every player and former players right to provide their own version of events."

In his new book, Khawaja said he was never spoken to despite sitting next to Cameron Bancroft during discussions about using sandpaper on the ball.

What did Khawaja say about Sandpapergate in his book? Much has been written and said about Usman Khawaja's new book — but what's actually in the pages of Sabr?

Cummins on Friday said he spoke to investigators and there were calls at the time for anyone with more information to come forward.

On Tuesday, Starc was one of the first players to be asked about Khawaja's claims and said there were "differing opinions of eight years ago".

"We were heavily grilled through the process at the time and since," he said.

"I won't speak on behalf of the bowlers but, from where I stand, my opinion hasn't changed, and my recollection hasn't changed from what we said in 2021."

In 2021, Bancroft implied in an interview that the bowlers likely knew what was going on.

"Obviously what I did benefits bowlers and the awareness around that, probably, is self-explanatory," he said.

Starc, Cummins, Lyon and Hazlewood released a joint statement in response, saying they were disappointed to have their integrity questioned.

"We did not know a foreign substance was taken onto the field to alter the condition of the ball until we saw the images on the big screen at Newlands," they wrote five years ago.

title: Hauser ends stunning triathlon season with silver
text:
Australia's leading triathlete Matt Hauser has claimed a silver medal in the season-ending World Triathlon Championship Series race in Abu Dhabi.

Gold Coast-based Hauser finished 18 seconds behind Brazil's Miguel Hidalgo, with New Zealand's Paris Olympics silver medallist Hayden Wilde in third.

The result confirms Hauser's second place finish in the overall season standings, with newly crowned world champion, Vasco Vilaça of Portugal, not racing in Abu Dhabi.

"I could really feel the legs in the back end of that race, I think I could feel the whole year in the back end of that race to be honest," said Hauser, who won four golds this season, as well as the Noosa Tri earlier this month.

"Miguel had too much out there today, you could tell he was really locked in and credit to him he did a lot of work on the bike as well.

"So all round a really great race and good to see him back on top as well."

The 'world champion persona' didn't come overnight for Matt Hauser Despite being Australia's first male triathlon world champion in 20 years, Matt Hauser is still building the blocks towards his aim of Olympic success in 2028.

The race, originally scheduled for March but postponed due to security concerns in the region, took place after the grand final in Pontevedra.

However, the competition still provided valuable qualifying points for the LA 2028 Olympic Games.

"I always think about LA, it's always in my mind, without overexposing my thoughts. It would be silly not to think about it," Hauser told AusTriathlon in the lead up to the Abu Dhabi event.

"It's a process and journey we've been on since Paris, I'm really focused on performing well at those Games."

The qualification period runs until May 18, 2028, with an athlete's 12 best results until then counting towards their overall ranking.

Fellow Australian Luke Willian came home in fifth place, with Luke Schofield 29th, Brandon Copeland 35th and Cal McClusky 40th.

"[It was good to see] Luke Willian having a sprint finish for fourth and fifth," Hauser said

"I'm just really stoked on the podium, it's been a big year and a long year at that."

Hayden Wilde (right) is shaping up as one of Matt Hauser's biggest challengers for Olympic gold in LA. (Supplied: World Triathlon)

In the women’s race, Matilda Offord was the best placed of the Australians finishing in 35th, with Sophie Malowiecki not finishing.

Russia's Diana Isakova claimed her first World Triathlon Series victory, surging away from Luxembourg's Jeanne Lehair, with American Gwen Jorgensen in third.

The race marks the end of the World Triathlon Series Championship races, as the tour combines with the Professional Triathletes Organisation to form a new Triathlon World Tour.

The new circuit will combined the existing T100 Triathlon World Tour and the World Triathlon Championship Series (WTCS), rebranded as the T100 World Championship Tour and T50 World Championship Tour respectively.

The Professional Triathletes Organisation (PTO) and World Triathlon today announced what the Triathlon World Tour brand will look like to fans and athletes when it starts next year, as well as the initial 2027 T50 and T100 World Championship Tour calendars.

"Our sport was really fragmented from a competition and commercial perspective, which was holding it back," World Triathlon president Antonio Arimany said earlier this year.

"We could have waited until the end of the current Olympic qualification before making the changes, but the changes we're making were too important to wait.

"By introducing the Triathlon World Tour now, we are creating one unified structure and brand, which can unify as many events as possible, creating a win-win situation for all of us in the sport."

title: What we know so far about why US flights were grounded
text:
The United States has lifted its order to ground departing flights nationwide as a major communications outage continues to disrupt air travel.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) cited "extraordinary circumstances and reasons of safety", with the White House blaming outdated air traffic control technology for the outage.

Thousands of flights into and out of the US were delayed or cancelled, leaving airlines and passengers scrambling to work out their next steps.

Look back on our live blog for the latest on the issues affecting flights in the US and Australia.

The ABC understands the US "ground stop" has caused some delays to a small number of US-bound flights from Australia.

Here's what we know about the unfolding situation so far.

What caused the problem?

US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has attributed the disruption to a telecommunications issue.

"It's just a telecommunications outage as of right now," Mr Mullin told reporters at the White House earlier on Friday, local time.

" Everybody's safe. There's no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying. "

It is not yet confirmed what specifically caused the communications failure.

Loading...

Mr Mullin had earlier said investigators would examine whether there was any connection to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence (AI) system designed to help identify problems and reroute aircraft.

However, the system operates from a single location near Washington DC and provides recommendations to air traffic control centres.

US President Donald Trump has also rejected suggestions the new AI technology was responsible for the disruption.

In his latest press conference, US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed "old technology" for the outage.

"What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system," he said.

"We have analogue telecoms, our routers actually got overloaded with data … and they started to give us inconsistencies in the data … because of that we shut the system down," he says.

" It is the old hardware that went down. "

Speaking to ABC News, Shawn Pruchnik, an associate professor in Ohio State University's aviation department, said officials made the right call by grounding departing aircraft as a precaution.

"We have this significant problem of airplanes at higher altitudes that cannot communicate with air traffic control, so the solution to that is less airplanes up there," he said.

"Keep everyone down, let everyone land."

Was it caused by a threat to the US?

Mr Mullin said there was currently no indication the outage was the result of a nefarious attack.

However, he later added:

"We're not ruling out anything at this point.

"The first thing is [to make sure] everybody that is flying in is safe."

In a subsequent press conference, Mr Mullin reiterated that there were no signs pointing to a cyber attack for now.

"Typically, somebody's going to raise their hand up and say, 'Hey, we did that'. There's no chatter. We haven't seen any footprints … of people that have got into the system," he said.

"It appears this was mechanically driven. However, we are still looking."

Is it linked to the Microsoft outage?

Microsoft has denied any known connection between its recent global outage and the FAA's nationwide stoppage.

"We have no indication that the FAA's nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services," the company said on X.

The statement came amid speculation about a possible link to Microsoft's 21-hour global outage, which was resolved earlier on Friday.

Mr Mullin also dismissed the suggestion of a connection, telling reporters: "I don't see any reason to connect those two at all."

Which flights were affected?

The FAA's order applied to departing flights across the US, grounding nearly all aircraft scheduled to take off during the five hours it was in effect.

The agency also asked Eurocontrol, its European counterpart, to suspend flights to the US from its 42 member states, including Türkiye, Morocco and Israel.

Aircraft that were already in the air when the order was issued were allowed to continue safely to their destinations.

The order to ground flights resulted in mass delays and flight cancellations. (AP Photo: Mike Stewart)

The full scale of the disruption is still emerging, but the impact has already been felt by tens of thousands of travellers.

Flight-tracking website FlightAware reported about 9,814 delays on flights into and out of the US, alongside more than 4,749 cancellations. Those figures are continuing to change as the disruption unfolds.

Meanwhile, the ABC understands Australian airlines are dealing with a backlog of delayed flights.

Australians caught in US flight chaos Thousands of flights have been delayed or cancelled across the US, leaving Australian travellers stranded at airports.

Before the US order was lifted, a Sydney Airports spokesperson had said all US-bound flights from Sydney were grounded.

Since the order was lifted, the spokesperson said:

"Flights scheduled to depart Sydney for the United States are expected to depart as planned. Passengers should continue to check with their airline for the latest information."

The ABC is continuing to stay in touch with Sydney Airports for further updates.

Can planes already in the air land safely?

Yes. Aviation experts say pilots and air traffic controllers are trained to manage communications failures.

Skip Bailey, an aviation professor who spoke to The Associated Press, said pilots were expected to maintain the headings and instructions given by air traffic controllers before communications were lost.

If the outage continued, they could revert to their filed flight plans.

Airlines and passengers were left scrambling to work out their next steps. (AP Photo)

Pilots may also be able to communicate with other aircraft over the radio, even if they cannot reach air traffic controllers. Commercial aircraft also have their own radar systems.

"It's not mass chaos out there," Professor Bailey said.

"There are plenty of ways to try to communicate."

He said preventing additional aircraft from taking off had been crucial to avoiding further complications.

"We don't want to put more aircraft into a system that's already having an issue."

When will flights resume?

Mr Duffy said US air space was reopened at 8:15pm Eastern Standard Time, about five hours after the grounding order was issued.

However, he warned that flights could be "slow" to take off again.

"If you are watching, if you are at an airport, check with your airline; it depends on [if they] have crews available," Mr Duffy said in his latest press conference.

"We are going to try to move as many of those [flights] as we can tonight if we have capacity.

"If not, we are going to start tomorrow morning with our airline partners to move those aircraft, but it is going to take us some time to unwind what has happened this afternoon."

The FAA has assured travellers the country is now safe for air travel.

"Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable," it said in a statement.

What's the advice for Australian travellers?

Australians travelling to the US should expect to hear from their airlines or travel agents as the disruption continues, the Australian Travel Industry Association said.

"We're absolutely expecting the domestic network within America to be disrupted for at least the next 24 hours," the industry body said in its latest statement.

"If you have a stand-by ticket, the reality is you probably aren't getting on a plane, but if you've got a confirmed ticket, you can rest assured those planes will be taking off safely and on time."
