title: 'Plastic farmers' in Indonesia unaware of the dangers of burning waste
text:
Ahmad Yani spent hours each day sifting through piles of rubbish, searching for recyclable materials to sell to help make ends meet.

For decades, his family and other people in his village in East Java in Indonesia would buy truckloads of waste residue from factories recycling imported paper and cardboard.

They would spread the waste on the ground, and separate plastics from paper and cardboard.

The paper would be sold back to the recycling factories and most of the plastics to industries that needed fuel for furnaces.

"It had become a source of livelihood for many low-income residents," Mr Yani said, adding he would make about 300,000 rupiah ($24) a month.

Any plastics still left over would be used in his village to fire limestone kilns, to produce building materials to sell or use.

Ahmad Yani says plastic waste from overseas has been coming to his village for decades. (Supplied: Brawijaya University)

Mr Yani said among the rubbish he noticed food sachets and cat and dog food packaging with Australian labels as well as labels of countries in Europe.

While burning plastic has helped support the family's livelihood, the smoke from their home and neighbouring households may be having devastating health impacts.

He said some people he knew who had operated the limestone kilns had died from respiratory diseases and causes were never determined.

Mr Yani said the burning of plastics in his village was no longer happening. It stopped about a year ago.

Several local media reported companies had stopped distributing waste to his community to sort, which had sparked anger among locals who lost their source of income.

The ABC couldn't independently verify the reasons for the change.

But health concerns for people who have been exposed to air pollution from burning plastics remain.

Women sort through waste in East Java. (Supplied: Brawijaya University)

'Unaware of the dangers'

Researchers from the Climate and Health Centre at Brawijaya University were investigating the health impacts of air pollution in East Java when they found locals were burning plastic waste.

One of the researchers, Sekar Aqila Salsabilla, said pre-screening tests earlier this year on those in their study produced some worrying findings.

She said at least 20 per cent of the more than 4,000 participants across six East Java villages were at high risk of cardiovascular disease and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

Sekar Aqila Salsabilla has been researching the health impacts of air pollution in villages in East Java. (Supplied: Sekar Aqila Salsabilla)

"When we first entered these communities, one of the most distressing findings was that many people were unaware of the dangers associated with burning plastic waste," said Ms Salsabilla, who worked with more than 30 researchers as part of a broader study, the majority of whom had medical backgrounds.

People earning money from sorting waste, known as "plastic farmers", knew their health was "slowly declining" but did not understand the source of the problems, she said.

"Despite the income they generate, many do not realise that the long-term health burden they may face is likely to be far greater than the money they earn from handling and burning this waste," Ms Salsabilla said.

Environmental activists say Australian plastic waste was in this rubbish heap in East Java, Indonesia, in 2024. (Supplied: Ecoton)

Most plastic waste was no longer burned in people's homes but rather converted into refuse-derived fuel (RDF) and burned in a designated facility, she said.

"But I think this only relocates the problem rather than actually solving it," Ms Salsabilla said, adding the facility still required humans to sort the waste.

Emissions from open waste burning, such as burning plastics, include a variety of air pollutants, some of which have particularly harmful effects on both the climate and health, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

"Exposure to these pollutants, whether short or long-term, can lead to adverse health effects such as coughing, skin irritation, respiratory diseases, and other negative outcomes," the WHO says on its website.

Environmentalists say plastic waste from Australia is often found in East Java. (Supplied: Ecoton)

Ms Salsabilla said the waste imported to East Java was coming from places including Australia, the US and Europe.

Agus Rusly, the waste reduction director at Indonesia's Ministry of Environment, told the ABC the lack of accessible waste management services, irregular waste collection, and limited recycling facilities had contributed to open waste burning in Indonesia.

Mr Rusly said the Environment Ministry was working to improve waste governance, in collaboration with regional governments, through a national framework "aimed at achieving comprehensive waste management by 2029".

Enforcement is 'weak'

In 2019, Indonesian environmentalists called on Australia to tighten its regulation and enforcement of waste exports to foreign countries, saying Australian exporters were effectively "smuggling" huge amounts of plastic and waste paper supposedly sent for recycling.

Daru Setyorini, executive director of local environmental activist group Ecoton, said plastics with Australian labels could still be found in East Java and people in villages were still "secretly" burning plastics.

Environmentalists have long called for Australia to tighten waste exports to countries such as Indonesia. (Supplied)

"To this day, it [the plastic waste] still exists, although it has decreased significantly compared to 2024 and the years before that," she said.

"The monitoring and enforcement are still weak. Ideally, these imports from Australia should just be stopped altogether."

Australia exported 701,000 tonnes of paper and cardboard to Indonesia in the recent financial year, according to Joe Pickin at Blue Environment who analysed data from Australia's Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW).

While Australia can legally export recyclable plastic waste to Indonesia, concerns have centred on plastic contaminants in paper and cardboard exports.

'Take your s*** from Indonesia' Environmentalists in Indonesia claim that among the thousands of tonnes of paper bales sent to East Java are household waste items including faeces-contaminated nappies.

Indonesia applies a 2 per cent contamination limit on paper waste imports, meaning contaminants such as plastic, food residue, soil and other non-paper materials must not exceed that threshold.

A spokesperson for Australia's Environmental Protection Authority (EPA) said it took "allegations of unlawful waste exports seriously".

"The National EPA assesses allegations of non-compliance with Commonwealth environmental laws and takes a proportionate, risk-based approach to determining appropriate regulatory responses," they said.

Many Australian material recovery facilities have invested significantly in upgrading their operations to meet these standards and ensure that materials exported for recycling met appropriate quality requirements, according to the Australian Council of Recycling.

"Failure to enforce these rules not only risks environmental harm but also disadvantages operators doing the right thing, undermining their investments," CEO Suzanne Toumbourou said.

Ms Setyorini said each country should be responsible for its own plastic waste.

"Indonesia has got enough waste problems, so developed countries like Australia shouldn't export their waste here," she said.

The DCCEEW has been contacted for comment.

title: The Townsville creatives making their own queer community
text:
Townsville is known for humidity, rugby league, and its unofficial status as North Queensland's capital.

Its queer culture is less visible, but that is changing as more people create the communities they once had to leave regional Queensland to find.

Michael Smith knows that experience well.

The professional dancer grew up in Gladstone before moving to Brisbane.

"Growing up as a queer person in a regional place, I didn't have any elders or community members to paint a picture of what a queer life could be," they said.

Mx Smith grew up in Gladstone before moving to Brisbane, but later returned to regional Queensland. (ABC News: Isabella Garrido)

Years later, Mx Smith returned to regional Queensland.

"There's actually a really large queer and trans community in Townsville," they said.

"There just aren't many things that are overtly visible that bring everyone together."

Finding a queer community did not necessarily mean Mx Smith found where they felt most at home.

Rather than leave, they began wondering how else a queer community could look.

Creating a new community

With writer P. Eldridge, they created CROOKED, an independent queer publication — due to launch on November 14 — rooted in Gurambilbarra, the traditional Wulgurukaba name for Townsville.

The project quickly revealed there were others also looking for a different way to connect.

Lij Bolden was one of them.

Lij Bolden participated in writing workshops to prepare their written piece for CROOKED. (ABC News: Emma Jones)

Writing for CROOKED gave Mx Bolden the chance to tramp down memory lane.

"It's peppered [with] vignettes of my life and realising I'm queer and discovering other people like me," they said.

They reflected on the parts of themself they had once kept hidden.

"I got to sit in that space and relive my queerness in a place where I did feel lonely and unseen, but realising that maybe I've had that queerness in me this entire time," Mx Bolden said.

Greater visibility, however, can come with risk.

"With the amount of political divisiveness and extremity in the world, it takes effort to be neutral," Mx Smith said.

" To be outwardly queer is already making a political statement, especially in a regional city. "

That risk became reality at a Townsville Pride event in June 2025, where Mx Smith was preparing to perform when a small group disrupted the event.

An attendee who asked the group to leave was allegedly assaulted.

"It had been a long time since I had felt that kind of hostility targeted towards a specific group of people," Mx Smith said.

The experience reinforced for them why visible signs of safety mattered.

"As a young queer person in a regional place, you can be hypervigilant in public, constantly assessing every room you step into, looking for danger and looking for safety," they said.

"If someone has gone to the effort of putting up a [pride] flag, it takes a little of that social anxiety and pressure off your shoulders."

Queensland Council for LGBTI Health chief executive Rebecca Reynolds agreed visible signs of welcome mattered but said what followed was just as important.

Rebecca Reynolds says belonging also means having room to be the whole of who you are. (Supplied: Queensland Council for LGBTI Health)

"Visible inclusion needs to lead to something people can use: a welcoming person, clear information, an activity they can join or help reaching the right support," she said.

Beyond pride events

Research suggests knowing a community exists is not necessarily the same as feeling part of it.

A 2025 University of Southern Queensland study of 87 LGBTQ+ people in the Toowoomba region found participants wanted safety, support, acceptance, friendship and connection.

Ms Reynolds said everyday recreational groups could foster connection across the year, beyond larger moments of visibility such as pride events.

"These spaces can take many forms, shaped by the people who use them. What matters is that people can find somewhere that feels right for them."

For Ms Eldridge, those spaces should grow from the places they serve.

Writer P. Eldridge helped create CROOKED, an independent queer publication. (Supplied: P. Eldridge)

"I'm deeply suspicious of the idea that interesting queer culture only happens in capital cities because it doesn't," they said.

"Gurambilbarra has its own queer histories, its own ways of surviving and making community that I think we, as a culture and a movement, can benefit from listening to.

"CROOKED came from wanting to listen to that rather than parachuting in with an idea of what regional queer life should look like."

Ms Eldridge said trans and queer writing had its own lineage, one that was still being defined, shaped and expanded.

"I believe that means there's no reason to confine ourselves. We can pretty much make anything new whenever we want," they said.

"I don't want to mitigate how dangerous regional life can be because of the backward turn toward fascism, but I will say that in the midst of so many crises, there is even more strength, solidarity and hope."

" Trans and queer people are the most resilient, there's no straightening us out. "

CROOKED, an independent queer publication, is due to launch on November 14. (Supplied)

Mx Smith said they felt a responsibility to make visible what they could not see growing up.

"CROOKED is the messier version of queerness," Mx Smith said.

"It's brash and it's not polished.

title: A friendship forged on the rugby league fields of New Zealand a century ago
text:
Awhina Hetet and Rita McRae Kingi share a drink on a blistering November day, on the balcony of Awhina's Logan business.

The women and their families met and became close mates in Brisbane, after moving to the city from Rotorua and Marton and in New Zealand.

But the families' close bond was first forged more than a century ago, on the rugby league fields of New Zealand.

Awhina's great-great-great grandfather Hōne Taonui "John" Hetet was the team manager for the Māori All Stars in 1909.

Hōne Taonui "John" Hetet was the team manager for the Maori All Stars in 1909. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

Rita's great-great grandfather Nirai Whareure "Ned" McRae was a coach, captain, and player.

The players had all anglicised their names before making the trip across the ditch for the campaign 117 years ago.

Hōne Taonui "John" Hetet (far left) was the team manager for the Maori All Stars in 1909 and Nirai Whareure "Ned" McRae (far right) was a coach, captain, and player. (Supplied)

"New Zealand was a nation of union players," Awhina says. "When they came over in 1909 to Australia … we brought with us our haka, our culture. They had two guides with them … they came with a campaign to show, 'this is who we are, we're Māori. We love this game.'"

"You see how proud they are and I think our people absolutely displayed that proudness when they put on the shirt."

Rob Hetet, Awhina Hetet, Rita McRae King, Te-Kapua Rahoroi Kingi and Harley Kingi. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

One of the guides was Mākereti "Maggie" Papakura, a Māori-English translator who was posthumously awarded a Master of Philosophy in Anthropology from the University of Oxford.

Mākereti "Maggie" Papakura, a Māori-English translator, was a guide. (Supplied)

At the time, rugby league was struggling financially in Australia. But the Aussie-Kiwi clashes attracted more than 30,000 to their games.

The Maori side left victorious, taking the cup back to New Zealand. It is now in the care of Awhina's family "in an undisclosed location," she laughs, in New Zealand.

Rob Hetet with the 1909 cup. (Supplied)

"That cup's still standing, it's one of the oldest rugby league cups in existence," she says.

"Beautiful history," adds her father, Rob Hetet. "That's probably why I am really passionate."

The Hetet family also has distant links to star Kiwi player Kalyn Ponga, who is part of the starting side for the World Cup Final in Brisbane this Sunday.

Te-Kapua Rahoroi Kingi, Harley Kingi and Rob Hetet. (ABC News: Curtis Rodda)

The Hetet and McRae families will be in the stands at Lang Park, with a closer link to the game than most other revellers.

"It's been 13 years since we were in the finals," says Awhina.

"Our boys have been amazing throughout this whole campaign … may the best team win!"

title: Minns vows to open 100 long-day childcare centres if re-elected
text:
The NSW government will open and operate 100 new long-day childcare centres to address demand if it wins the state election in March.

The centres are in addition to an existing government pledge to build 100 new preschools and have them operational from January next year.

In the private sector, long-day centres offer early childhood services for children from birth to four years old and operate between 7am and 6pm.

The announcement on Saturday from the Minns government will deliver the first publicly owned long-day childcare centres in NSW, providing 5,000 places for about 8,000 families.

Chris Minns expects many long-day centre locations to open up in Western Sydney. (ABC News)

Premier Chris Minns said the centres would be built on existing public primary school sites and in areas deemed so-called childcare deserts.

He said the government would "not be indiscriminate" about new locations and that he expected many to open in Western Sydney and regional NSW.

"The reality is, for us in New South Wales, if we want a productive economy, we want to make sure that we're giving every family the opportunity to get ahead," Mr Minns said.

" So many people are missing out and they're missing out for the most obvious reasons [and] that is that after they have a child, they can't get affordable child care. "

Prue Car says families are in desperate need of extended child care hours. (ABC News)

Deputy Premier Prue Car said families desperately needed the extended care hours the centres would provide.

"That will end the double drop off and it will make it easier for parents to get back into the workforce," she said.

"It will also create an opportunity for high quality early learning as children transition into kindergarten and primary school."

Funding guarantee for community preschools

The government will also extend the transitional funding period for community run preschools.

As part of the NSW government's early childhood education reforms, the Universal Preschool Funding Program will replace the Start Strong arrangement from January 1.

According to the government, 10,000 families are missing out on the community preschool places, which are not-for profit.

"We have listened to the concerns of the sector, and we've responded to that by guaranteeing their funding for two years," Mr Minns said on Saturday.

Doubts over key date for 100 new preschools The opening of a new preschool in Sydney's south-west has raised questions over plans to expand preschools in NSW.

"That will freeze their funding at, at least, last year's level.

"So that will give community preschools a funding guarantee that they will not go backwards while we work with them on how we can get more children into their high quality preschool."

Carol Matthews from the Independent Education Union of Australia said preschools had been "extremely worried" about losing thousands of dollars in funding next year, and prior to today's announcement had started to shed staff.

"Now obviously, this reprieve is really going to help, but nevertheless, there's been significant damage done already," the union's NSW ACT branch secretary said.

While the union welcomed the election promise, Ms Matthews said there was "more work to do on the details of the model".

"We want them [the NSW government] to sit down with us, and actually negotiate an outcome which would enable some sort of stability and security in staffing going forward.

"That means recognising the actual staffing needs of preschools."

title: PearlBone gets FDA clearance for world's largest orthopaedic market
text:
Mother-of-pearl harvested in Western Australia's north could soon be used to fill bone fractures for patients in the United States.

WA biotech company Marine Biomedical has received clearance from the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for its bone graft substitute, PearlBone.

A manufacturing facility for PearlBone was built in Broome in 2022. (Supplied: Rolee Kumar)

The product is the first of its kind to be developed from nacre, commonly known as mother-of-pearl.

The iridescent material has been used for ornamental items, jewellery and even buttons.

But Marine Biomedical chief executive Rolee Kumar said it was also effective for bone repair and regeneration.

PearlBone will be used to repair bone fractures for patients in the United States. (Supplied: Rolee Kumar)

"The material of what the mother-of-pearl is made out of, all of these are actually building blocks of our bone too," she said.

"So in a way, it's not surprising when we do these studies we see PearlBone facilitates bone healing."

The United States is the world's largest orthopaedics market, with the bone grafts and substitutes sector valued at $US1.1 billion ($1.5 billion).

Ms Kumar said FDA clearance was an important first step in entering the US market, but there were more hurdles to be overcome before it could be sold.

Rolee Kumar says PearlBone is as safe and effective as existing bone repair materials. (Supplied: Rolee Kumar)

"We've gone through a process where PearlBone was compared against another existing bone graft that's established itself in the market," she said.

"We've been able to demonstrate PearlBone is as safe and efficacious as the predicate device."

She said the company also hoped to bring the product to Australian customers in future and expand into other treatments like dental work.

'Exciting' opportunity for pearl industry

Marine Biomedical was established in 2021 through a partnership with local Broome pearling business Willie Creek Pearls and research expertise from the University of Western Australia (UWA).

Paul Birch says shells are prepped at the farm before being transported to the manufacturing facility in Broome. (Supplied: Willie Creek Pearls)

Willie Creek chief executive Paul Birch said the collaboration was an exciting opportunity for the pearling industry.

"I think it just opens everyone's eyes to what can potentially be done," he said.

"And with more research, there might be other parts of the oyster that can be used for other biomedical technologies."

The shells farmed by Willie Creek for pearl production undergo cleaning and preparations before being transported to the Marine Biomedical manufacturing facility in Broome.

Mr Birch said there was an abundance of pearl shell available at the farm to meet current requirements, but this could change as the product demand increased.

"So hopefully at one point in time, it might be something the entire industry is able to be involved in and supply to Marine Biomedical," he said.

The shell is harvested at Willie Creek Pearls, off the Kimberley coast. (Supplied: Willie Creek Pearls)

UWA biomedical and health innovation director Kevin Pfleger said it was an exciting time for medical research in WA.

"Often people don't realise we have some amazing innovations which are changing the world," he said.

The professor said it was common for products to gain approval in the United States market before returning to Australia.

"One of the big reasons is because even though we're a very large country geographically, we've got a relatively small population," Professor Pfleger said.

"So if we get approval in the US first, it means it's much more economically viable for us to then come back and market in Australia."

Willie Creek Pearls, based on the outskirts of Broome in WA's north, will provide the product for PearlBone. (ABC Kimberley: Ben Collins)

Professor Pfleger said the clearance was an "inspiring" achievement for others in the industry.

"The next point is obviously making sales, getting patients and benefiting from that and getting surgeons using it," he said.

"But regulatory approval is critical."

title: Do Australians actually want cheaper housing? We're finding out fast
text:
Australia's housing crisis has entered a new phase: a little less conversation, a little more action.

The first seeds were planted three years ago, with a landmark national agreement to build more homes. The target, 1.2 million in five years, is likely doomed. But what mattered was that a target was set at all. After years of lip service, leaders had promised to act on the root cause.

Then there was last year's economic roundtable. After much fanfare, the closed-door event had seemed like a fizzer. But for Treasurer Jim Chalmers, it helped build the case that Labor's old policy to wind back negative gearing could be reinvented, and framed as a leg up for home buyers over investors.

A policy to boost supply and a policy to slash demand. Throw in the highest interest rates in 18 years, and all of a sudden a housing market that seemed as if it would never turn is turning very fast indeed. This week saw the steepest drop-off in new home loans ever recorded.

How house and unit values compare in 2026 Unit values outperform houses in most capital cities as rising interest rates shrink borrowing power and reshape demand.

Commentators had long wondered whether, for all the hand-wringing about the housing crisis, Australians would actually want a solution when it came, since, one way or another, cheaper homes for the young can only mean less valuable homes for those who already own them.

But no more need to wonder: we're finding out. A tumbling market may not have been federal Labor's ideal pathway to affordable housing, but after months of dithering, the government took a tentative step this week towards embracing the chaos, framing it as a win for homebuyers.

In the coming weeks and months, Labor governments in Australia's two largest states will put their own higher-density plans to voters. At federal and state levels, Liberals are betting voters will dislike the prescribed cure worse than the sickness.

A falling knife

Labor did not expect its changes to the capital gains tax and negative gearing to tank house prices. Treasury analysis predicted prices would still grow, but by 2 per cent less. Chalmers has repeatedly said he is "not targeting a particular price".

Nor did it want prices to tank. In 2024, Housing Minister Clare O'Neil said it was her "strong view" that falling prices would be bad.

"Our policies are not going to reduce house prices. We want house prices to grow sustainably," she said then.

Clare O'Neil has been caught between championing affordability and protecting people's investments. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

But now they have fallen. The median national house price is 5.6 per cent below its March peak, and 3.9 per cent for apartments. The drop-off has been sharper in Melbourne and Sydney, and some analysts predict double-digit declines.

Other indicators point in the same direction. The auction clearance rate has plunged below 50 per cent, compared to its long-run average of 60 per cent. And new figures this week showed a record 15 per cent dip in new loans between June and September.

The chill was evident across the board, but it was clearly worse for investors (31 per cent) than for homebuyers (5 per cent). First home buyers (8 per cent) fared worse than established homebuyers, but still far better than investors.

High rates have clearly played a role. But they do not explain why investors are falling away by "so much more than in previous interest rate increasing cycles", as Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock observed last week.

"[That] suggests something else is going on here, and [that] is the tax changes," she said. In other words, the tax changes are doing what they were designed to do: discourage investors.

Until this week, the government had been skittish about embracing that. Even after opinion polls suggested a majority of Australians believed that prices needed to fall, ministers were nervous about embracing the nosedive.

But on Wednesday, O'Neil ditched the script and stopped equivocating.

Essential workers priced out of housing Research shows nurses, teachers and social workers can only afford a small percentage of rental listings across Australia.

"We've had a housing market geared towards investors for a generation, and where did it get us? Plummeting ownership, out-of-control house price increases, and a generation losing hope," she said.

"These numbers show the balance is shifting back … It is absolutely the case that volumes are down, as you would expect in a period where prices are softening. But these figures also clearly show a strong shift away from investors and towards Australians buying a home to live in."

It is a risky gambit. First home buyers may be getting a leg up — CBA's Matt Comyn said yesterday their share of new loan applications doubled last month. But a fast-falling market is a risky one to enter, especially with high rates, and it can also chill housing supply.

Liberal housing spokesperson Andrew Bragg seized on the comments, calling them "strange".

"People would look at what Clare O'Neil says and think, 'Well, what planet is she living on? Why is she saying fewer loans is good?' Fewer loans is bad [sic]. We need to see more lending."

A chorus of real estate moguls and personal finance celebrities agree. A prominent example is podcaster Mark Bouris, who predicted in The Australian this week "the longest downturn in our history" and warned: "We're going to have a serious structural hit to people's wealth."

Loading

The supply side

The comments are revealing, hinting at what motivates many critics. Not affordability, but wealth.

That cannot be said of Bragg, one of a handful of politicians who have publicly embraced the idea that lower house prices could be welcome if they happen via a supply boom, not a demand chill.

But for many home owners, wealth is front of mind, and this is just as true on the supply side as it is on the demand side, as state governments are finding out.

In Victoria, the Labor government has pursued the most aggressively pro-supply policy in the country, designating several Melbourne suburban hubs as so-called "activity centres", where high-density towers will be allowed in narrow strips and medium density in wider surrounds.

Typical of the cynical political style of former premier Daniel Andrews and his successor Jacinta Allan, many zones are in places Labor will never win, including in Brighton and state Liberal leader Jess Wilson's Kew.

Jess Wilson said a Coalition government would shift the focus of high-rise development to Melbourne's CBD and inner city. (ABC News)

Locals have been whipped into a frenzy by dystopian artists' impressions of amorphous black skyscrapers invading their leafy shopping strips, a feature of media coverage.

Kew and Brighton will hardly shape the election, which pundits predict Labor will lose for other reasons, but Wilson has vowed to scrap the plan and give local councils a veto if elected.

A similar dynamic is emerging in Sydney, where the Minns Labor government will face voters early in the new year and where designated density zones in suburbs like Woollahra and Crows Nest are also opposed by the opposition leader, Kellie Sloane.

Sloane, echoing Wilson and many Teal MPs, says she supports more housing but frames her complaint as one of consultation and is also promising a council veto.

The argument has a reasonable-sounding guise — "We just want locals to have a say" — but to pro-supply campaigners like Peter Tulip, it is an all-too-familiar smokescreen for building fewer homes, since councils make decisions for existing residents, not potential new ones.

"[The] households who move in would be better off. As would renters and homebuyers who benefit from improved affordability. They greatly outnumber the opponents, but they don't get to vote for the local politicians who are biased against new housing," he said last week.

If Tulip is right, the political numbers game should favour Labor governments at federal and state levels if their policies really do make housing more affordable: they would lose Kew and Crows Nest, but win the country.

In different economic and political circumstances, that reckoning might have come gradually. Instead, we are hurtling towards it.

title: Albanese, Bowen caught talking phones and 'dicks' in hot-mic gaffe
text:
A conversation between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen about phone radiation and "dicks" has been caught on camera on the sidelines of a UN conference.

Mr Albanese's office said the pair was sharing a "joke" between meetings when the exchange was recorded by Australian media at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye.

The comments were captured shortly before a business roundtable spruiking renewable energy transition investment opportunities in Australia began overnight on Friday.

Anthony Albanese left Türkiye shortly after a business roundtable. (AAP)

Cameras were rolling ahead of the event during which time Mr Albanese and Mr Bowen were privately chatting to each other.

Mr Albanese put his phone in his jacket pocket and — as he did so — told Mr Bowen he had heard it was better to store the device away from the heart because "it can interfere with your rhythm".

Mr Bowen responded in a joking tone if it was because the phone was "a little bit radioactive".

The prime minister laughed, saying the idea "makes absolute sense". Mr Bowen then responded he was more conscious about putting his phone in his pants pocket. Mr Albanese asked, "Because of your dick?" The pair laughed and Mr Bowen agreed, adding it was "arguably more important than the heart".

Hot-mic gaffe came ahead of roundtable

The exchange, which did not appear to be overheard by anyone in the room but was captured by a news camera microphone preparing to record the opening remarks at the event, was later broadcast by Channel 7 after it was noticed in production.

A spokesperson for Mr Albanese's office said, "They were having a joke in between meetings."

Labor frontbencher Murray Watt agreed that the comments were made in jest.

"This is really just about people having a joke," he said.

While Mr Watt laughed off a question about where he keeps his own phone, and defended Australia's presence and performance at COP31.

"I know there's been a lot of criticism from some quarters about every aspect of this COP, but the reality is participating in and in fact leading the discussions at COP is in Australia's national interest," he said.

During the official proceedings of the business roundtable, the prime minister made a pitch to international investors to back Australia's clean energy transition.

"If you're an investor, there's nowhere you'd rather be than Australia," he said.

Mr Albanese said having abundant renewable resources, critical minerals and a stable investment environment meant Australia was well placed to capitalise on the multi-trillion-dollar industry.

The prime minister left Türkiye shortly after the roundtable to travel to the Philippines for the ASEAN summit in Manila.

Mr Bowen has remained in Antalya, where he is playing a critical role as the co-president of negotiations for COP31.

title: Questions remain after Nvidia CEO's departure
text:
Mounting speculation over an espionage plot against Jensen Huang and his multiple alleged affairs reached a tipping point on Friday, when the tech billionaire quit as Nvidia's CEO.

The controversy centred around his relationship with Alice Huang, who US intelligence reportedly suspects to be a Chinese spy, before claims emerged he had another two extra-marital affairs.

While Mr Huang's resignation puts an end to his long reign over Nvidia, questions about America's national security and the US president's knowledge of the whole saga remain.

China's foreign ministry said allegations of spying in relation to Alice Huang and Jensen Huang (no relation) were "unsubstantiated" and "smears against China". (Reuters: CTI)

Questions for Jensen Huang

When reports of an espionage plot against Mr Huang first emerged almost a week ago, top Republicans called on the tech executive to front Congress later this month.

Senator Tim Scott reiterated those demands after Mr Huang's resignation, saying there were "serious concerns" to address.

Separately the chairs of three House committees — the foreign affairs panel, the China select committee and the intelligence committee — wrote to Mr Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter requiring them to appear for closed-door transcribed interviews on December 1 and 2.

Who is Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang? After news broke of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset Nvidia's value plummeted. Why?

Mr Huang and Mr Teter have not publicly commented on the requests, but they could face subpoenas to compel their appearances.

"There are clear national security concerns that need to be addressed immediately," the three committee chairs wrote in the letter.

Mr Huang is also yet to comment publicly after reports emerged he allegedly had another two extra-marital affairs — both with Nvidia employees.

His last statement was on Sunday, local time, when he admitted to being "unfaithful" to his wife of over 40 years but did not name who he had been intimate with.

In that statement, he said he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security".

Meanwhile, Nvidia and Mr Huang are facing a ‌proposed class action accusing them ‌of ⁠defrauding ‌shareholders.

Questions for the US administration

Next to Mr Huang, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has been called on to testify in front of Congress on concerns he did not do enough to restrict AI chip shipments to China.

In December 2025 Donald Trump allowed Nvidia to sell its advanced chips to China in exchange for a cut of the sales, after Mr Huang argued that restrictions only accelerated Beijing's own AI development.

That was despite concerns from both sides of Congress about China's access to the technology.

Howard Lutnick is facing pressure over whether the US government was properly overseeing Nvidia's exports to China. (Reuters: Elizabeth Frantz)

Mr Lutnick has also been criticised for the administration's refusal to add dozens of Chinese companies to a trade blacklist.

In June, Reuters reported the Trump administration had held ⁠off adding more than 100 other companies flagged as national security risks to the list.

The US ⁠has not added to the list since October 2025, the longest stretch between new postings in more than a decade.

Previous reports said that Mr Lutnick's US Commerce Department had not blacklisted new Chinese companies for fear of escalating tensions between the US and China.

Under-Secretary of Commerce Jeffrey Kessler has been called on to testify at a December 3 hearing as well.

"Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under-Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fuelling China's military," Democrat Senator Elizabeth Warren said.

The Commerce Department did not respond to Reuters' request for comment.

Questions for Donald Trump

In America's pursuit to lead the AI race, Mr Huang had become a close ally of Mr Trump and was one of the few people known to have a direct line to him.

He has visited the White House at least five times during Mr Trump's second term, is part of a council advising the president on science and technology, and accompanied Mr Trump on a trip to Beijing in May.

Loading...

The Washington Post reported in mid-October that Nvidia committed $US25 million ($36.7 million) for Mr Trump's contentious White House ballroom project, while the president disclosed buying and selling Nvidia stock earlier this year.

The New York Times reported Mr Trump was briefed on intelligence findings about a suspected espionage effort against Mr Huang about a year ago, and took no action.

When asked in recent days whether he wished he had acted sooner on that information, Mr Trump said "I don't think so" and maintained that Mr Huang was an "honourable guy".

The president has continued to stand by Mr Huang and said the tech billionaire told him he had no idea Ms Huang was a spy, and that he believed him.

Questions for Nvidia

On the day Mr Huang admitted to his affair, Nvidia announced it had called an independent investigation into whether their then-chief executive had been the "target of a foreign intelligence effort".

But early in the piece, the company said it had "no reason to believe" either US national security or company secrets had been compromised.

There was no mention of the investigation when Nvidia announced its current executive vice-president and chief financial officer Colette Kress was stepping in as interim CEO.

Instead, Nvidia's new chair Harvey C Jones said: "We expect the company's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption."

It remains to be seen as to whether the investigation finds evidence Mr Huang gave away sensitive information — or whether its findings are publicly revealed.

Loading...

Questions for Alice Huang and Megaspeed

Ms Huang, who's been identified as a former executive at Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, has not commented publicly since the Nvidia scandal erupted.

Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy The chief executive of the world's most valuable company and a close ally of Donald Trump admitted to an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. Here's what we know.

China has denied she is a spy and US Attorney-General Todd Blanche said on Thursday the Justice Department had not yet reached a conclusion on whether she was or not.

Last year, Megaspeed was accused of illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December said there was "no evidence" of such exports.

Singaporean authorities also said they questioned Ms Huang and confiscated her passport last year as part of an investigation into Megaspeed's exports.

They concluded there wasn't enough evidence that she had committed a crime, but suspected she provided "inaccurate information" to downplay her role at Megaspeed.

Ms Huang left Singapore in February when she received her passport back and was banned from re-entering the country.

She is currently living in Beijing with the knowledge of security officials, Bloomberg News reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

The Singapore home affairs ministry said investigations into Megaspeed and six individuals were ongoing.

Megaspeed said on Thursday it took compliance obligations under US export control laws "extremely seriously", adding it had cooperated with US inspections.

ABC/Reuters/AP

title: Australia wins six Youth Olympics medals as African Games hailed
text:
Australia has come away from the 2026 Youth Olympic Games with six medals as Senegal held up its hands for the Olympic movement in Africa.

The Dakar Games were the first Olympic event to be hosted in Africa, with organisers hailing the success as further proof of the continent's ability to host major international competitions.

South Africa, which staged the men's FIFA World Cup in 2010, is among countries in talks with the IOC about hosting the 2036 Olympic Games.

Nearly 2,700 athletes aged 14 to 17 competed across 25 sports and 153 medal events over two weeks in Senegal.

"I think that everyone came here with certain expectations and I think those expectations have been far exceeded," International Olympic Committee President Kirsty Coventry said on Thursday.

"It has been an magnificent journey. It has been extremely magical.

"I think we've shown the world the capability that we have and now we need to choose to take that forward," the Zimbabwean two-time Olympic champion added.

Australia's six medals included four silvers and two bronzes.

Boxer Marley Dodd claimed silver in the men's 55kg event, while Mackenzie Macdonald claimed Australia's first ever taekwondo Youth Olympic Games medal in the 49kg category.

Marley Dodd won silver on the penulimate day of the competition. (Supplied: AOC)

Australia's cyclists excelled, with Elsie Apps winning silver and Caleb McKenzie bronze on the same day in the women's and men's road races.

Tasmania's McKenzie, who was diagnosed with the autoimmune illness Hashimoto’s disease earlier this year, led the race via a brave breakaway right up until the final lap before sprinting for bronze.

"I wasn't on the bike for a long time," McKenzie told Olympics.com.

"I couldn't ride my bike, I couldn't train and nothing really went well for me.

Caleb McKenzie rode in the breakaway for the majority of the men's road race. (Supplied: AOC)

"I finally pulled it together at the end of this year and had a really good ride. I had the confidence. We talked about it before we raced about having confidence in yourself, and we said, 'If you believe, you achieve'."

Apps, meanwhile, sprinted to silver.

"I'm so grateful for the opportunity that I was given to be able to go out there and get a medal," Apps said.

"It's been really inspiring. To have a little taste of what it would be like, it really makes you want more and hopefully I can make it there [to Brisbane 2032]."

Elsie Apps came second in the women's road race. (Supplied: AOC)

Queensland's beach volleyball pairing Thomas Turner and Ryan Edgar won bronze, while the women's rugby sevens teams were only denied gold in an extra-time thriller against Kenya, which claimed a first ever Olympic rugby sevens title for the nation.

Apps and Dodd were named as closing ceremony flag bearers, with Chef de Mission Kenny Wallace said the success gave him a lot of positivity heading to Brisbane 2032.

"To summarise the last two weeks … it would come down to being proud," he said.

"I'm inspired by what our Australian sporting ecosystem has in store leading into LA28 and into Brisbane 2032.

"When we came into this campaign, we hoped Dakar would become that important milestone for our emerging athletes with Brisbane 2032 on the horizon.

"It's been incredibly inspiring to see the athletes developing even further here in Dakar and understanding what it means to be part of an Australian team.

"That is what a Youth Olympic Games can do. I really look forward to seeing some of the faces that we've had in the team here in Brisbane."

First African Games hailed but future questioned

Elisabeth Diatta was one of Senegal's gold medal winners at her country's first home Olympic event. (Getty Images: Francois Nel)

Beach wrestling's Olympic debut brought particular pride to Senegal, where wrestling is a national sport, with 16-year-old Elisabeth Diatta's win the first for the host nation.

Other Youth Olympic debuts included baseball5, a simplified version of baseball, skateboarding, and the Chinese martial art wushu.

China finished with the most gold medals, 18, followed by Japan with 11 and Russia with eight.

Three African countries came next: Egypt with six, and Ethiopia and Senegal with five each.

The IOC staged the first summer Youth Olympic Games in 2010 in Singapore, however it has delayed naming the host for the next event, set to take place in 2030.

Kirsty Coventry hailed Africa's first Olympic event. (Supplied: AOC)

"We took a pause … and we are analysing and that's where we are. We are still analysing. The data we will collect from Dakar will be added," Coventry said.

"As we move forward, the way we want to engage with young people is extremely important. We have to analyse what will be the best way for the movement to continue in the future."

Coventry noted that just 15 per cent of athletes who have competed at the Youth Olympic Games have gone on to compete at the full Olympics.

Jess Fox and Emma McKeown are notable Australians who made the leap, winning gold at the Youth Olympic Games before going on to claim 20 Summer Olympic Games medals between them.

"We have to be very realistic about what we want the Youth Olympics to be," Coventry said.

ABC/wires

title: Regional bands say it's now cheaper to do a gig in London than interstate
text:
With the cost of regional airfares soaring, musicians and band managers say touring has become untenable for both famous bands and emerging artists from regional Australia.

An interim Productivity Commission report released this week revealed a significant price gap between regional and metropolitan flight routes.

It found long regional and remote flights cost 67 per cent more on average than major city routes, while short regional flights cost 173 per cent more per kilometre.

Alan James says high airfares are pricing Yothu Yindi "out of the market" for live music. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Yothu Yindi manager Alan James said the cost of travel had forced the internationally-renowned band from Arnhem Land to turn down shows within Australia.

"It's $5,200 return from Gove to Brisbane, it would be cheaper for us to go do a concert in London than it would be to do a concert in a capital city of Australia," he said.

" It's just pricing us out of the market. "

Yothu Yindi bassist Stuart Kellaway — who now manages fellow Arnhem Land rock band King Stingray — said the next generation band's recent flights to shows in the United States cost less than domestic flights.

Yothu Yindi played the 2025 Garma Festival but had to turn down shows interstate. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"We've had to turn down three or four shows in the past month or so because it just wasn't going to work financially with the airfare components," he said.

Mr Kellaway the sky-high airfares were affecting the ability even of artists in the prime of their careers to make a living.

"With streaming and everything else, gigs are one of the last, decent income streams for bands," he said.

Limited options limiting opportunities

Mr James said while all bands were impacted by the exorbitant airfares, for new artists in particular, the costs could make sustainable careers in the music industry impossible.

"If you're an emerging group, you've got no shot, you're out of the business," he said.

"It really means for musicians, if you're not based in a capital city, then you're not in the market anymore."

King Stingray manager Stuart Kellaway (third from left) says bands based outside capital cities are "not in the market anymore". (ABC / Matt Garrick)

Both Mr James and Mr Kellaway said they had noticed a decline in the number of airlines servicing Arnhem Land throughout the course of Yothu Yindi's career.

Their observations align with the findings of the Productivity Commission's report, which noted competition in regional aviation was severely limited.

Skyrocketing regional airfares hurting patients Fears FIFO specialists will soon need to pass rising flight costs onto vulnerable country patients.

Several airlines have reduced NT services recently, leaving flights between Darwin and capitals such as Sydney, Adelaide and Canberra serviced only by Qantas and its subsidiary Jetstar.

In a statement, a Qantas spokesperson said rising costs had dramatically influenced the price of tickets in and out of the NT.

"Aviation costs, including labour, airport charges and government air traffic control fees, are rising faster than the rate of inflation, while fuel costs also remain significantly higher," they said.

"Great value fares can still be found on flights to and from the Northern Territory and we encourage customers to book ahead whenever possible to secure the best fare."

title: Rope barriers at parliament round out prickly week for government
text:
If the government wanted to signal it was in touch with community concerns, walking through Hollywood-style velvet ropes and gold posts at parliament was probably not the best way to do it.

The ritzy accoutrements, aimed at separating politicians from the media as they arrive at parliament, seem more "let them eat cake" than cozzie living.

It was an image the government could have done without as it closed out a particularly challenging week.

Media barriers

Let's start with the extraordinary scenes of Labor MPs trying to shepherd their colleague, Riverton MP Jagadish Krishnan, past waiting media and into parliament.

Journalists have been asking MPs questions at that entrance for decades.

It's not the only way into the building, but it's often the only one media are waiting at.

Colleagues shielded Labor MP Jags Krishnan from the media on Wednesday. (ABC News)

Which makes it all the more extraordinary that when Dr Jags, as he's known, chose to walk through that entrance, MP Terry Healy tried to get between his beleaguered colleague and reporters before fellow MP Pierre Yang tried to pull him through the doorway.

The contribution of Cockburn MP David Scaife, who told reporters to be "ashamed of yourselves", didn't help — although he apologised the following day, saying he had been worried about politicians' safety claiming the entry was blocked by the media.

When the barriers were installed the following day by parliamentary staff, not a single MP who spoke that morning was supportive of them.

The rope barriers were seemingly intended to prevent journalists from getting too close to MPs as they entered the building. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

The premier's office subsequently admitted one of its staff had asked two unnamed MPs to "support" Dr Jags on his way into parliament.

"This is now a government with total contempt for transparency," opposition leader Basil Zempilas said.

"They have lost a handle on how to act, both in the chamber, outside the chamber, and with just about everything that they do."

Optics of restricting media

The issue of course isn't really the barriers — which are more of a symbolic than practical obstruction — or whether MPs like the media or not.

It's about the ability for an issue in the public interest — the business dealings and disclosures of Dr Jags — to be fully ventilated, and the appearance which is created when that doesn't happen.

Dr Jags Krishnan in parliament. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

The former GP is being sued in the United States over accusations of failing to pay back a million-dollar loan, which he's vowed to "vigorously defend".

Reporting in other media — which has not been verified by the ABC — has also raised questions about whether Dr Jags complied with the rules by telling parliament about his debts and any gifts he receives.

The opportunity to ask him directly about those issues was lost when he was swept into parliament.

The next day, during an ill-fated bid by the opposition to force an inquiry into the issues, Dr Jags said he was in the final process of selling a network of doctors' surgeries he had built and that "all outstanding matters will be resolved upon settlement".

"I have taken legal advice about my parliamentary declarations and I am confident that these are in order," he added.

Child protection sore point

The other lingering headache for the government is its handling of issues in the child protection system, first brought to light by media reports more than two months ago.

Some progress was made when Cook and Child Protection Minister Jessica Stojkovski met with Dorothy Papertalk, who says the system failed her three grandchildren before they were murdered by their mother.

But those problems do not begin or end in the child protection system, which is why elders and the opposition started questioning what role Aboriginal Affairs Minister Don Punch was playing in improving the lot for First Nations communities.

On Monday the premier denied it had taken Punch months to visit Port Hedland, before his minister admitted later that day it was his first visit since July.

The pair eventually managed to explain Punch's role in listening to Aboriginal communities and providing that information to cabinet, but couldn't really explain what difference that had made.

Don Punch admitted he hadn't been to Port Hedland since July. (ABC News: Briana Shepherd)

On Thursday he quoted from Pilbara Indigenous leader, Doris Eaton, who wrote that his attendance at an on-country meeting was "greatly appreciated" and a "great example" of collaboration.

But he failed to mention less favourable parts of that letter, including a section which notes her requests from 2024 and 2025 "are yet to be fully addressed or realised" and encouraging him to share her "concerns" with colleagues to instigate "much needed action".

On the backfoot

The government was left on the backfoot this week, forced to defend longstanding issues instead of focusing on anything constructive it was doing.

"I want to be talking about cost of living, health and housing, that's my priorities and that's what it will always be," minister John Carey said on Thursday.

John Carey speaks to journalists outside WA parliament, after the rope barriers were set up. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

And there is plenty to talk about in that space, including concern that the federal government's negative gearing changes may reduce rental supply.

It's yet another potential challenge facing the government at the end of a year which has grown increasingly difficult, after it lost a heartland seat in Secret Harbour to One Nation and struggled to gain support for its university merger proposal.

The summer break presents an opportunity to reset and return with a fresh focus in the new year.

For Labor, that can't come soon enough.

title: Australian cricket urged to stop 'eating itself' as Sandpapergate rolls on
text:
Greg Chappell has urged Australia's past and present cricket stars to end their civil war as the ghosts of Sandpapergate continue to haunt the game.

Usman Khawaja sent the cricket world into a spin last week when he claimed the ball tampering scandal in Cape Town in 2018 was everyone in the team's responsibility.

Cameron Bancroft, who was in charge of using sandpaper to roughen up one side of the ball, copped a nine-month ban in the wake of the cheating scandal, while Steve Smith and David Warner were suspended for a year and stripped of their leadership roles.

The fallout continues to this very day.

Test skipper Pat Cummins delivered an extraordinary 70-minute press conference in Sydney on Friday where he provided an open floor for journalists to ask whatever they wanted in regards to Sandpapergate 2018 and ball tampering in general, among other hot topics.

The 33-year-old steadfastly rejected claims he had any prior knowledge of the 2018 plot to use sandpaper on the ball in order to gain reverse swing.

He also hit out at Khawaja, saying the accusations were "complete nonsense" and suggested they were "probably defamatory".

Warner returned serve just hours after the press conference, saying he stood by all of Khawaja's claims and wouldn't rest until the full truth came out.

The former Test opener also accused Cummins of throwing Khawaja under the bus with his sandpaper denials.

Usman Khawaja has stood by his comments. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

Chappell knows a thing or two about controversy.

In 1981, and with NZ requiring six runs off the final ball to force a draw in a one-day match at the MCG, then-Australia captain Chappell ordered his younger brother Trevor Chappell to bowl the last delivery underarm.

While technically legal at the time, the move caused a massive backlash and forced a rule change, with the incident still brought up to this very day.

"Good luck with that. I think 45 years tells me it will probably be a while before it gets trumped," Chappell replied when asked if 'Sandpapergate' had finally trumped the underarm controversy.

"Mistakes have been made, I think you have to own them.

Cummins faces the music In his detailed 70-minute press conference, Pat Cummins said he hoped he could draw a line under the brewing Sandpapergate civil war. David Warner quickly proved that won't be happening.

"It would've been a tough time back in 2018 with all of that going on. I don't think you're always ready for these disasters when they happen, but we all make mistakes and they're all human beings.

"They're going to make mistakes, and I think we have to accept that and own those decisions, as I had to do 45 years ago."

Chappell doesn't want the in-fighting in Australian cricket to continue.

"We don't want to see Australian cricket eating itself and having a little spat within the family," Chappell said.

"Hopefully Pat's put a bit of a line under it and we can start getting on with the summer of cricket.

"It'll be a distraction, but I think they've all had enough experience that when they walk out on the cricket field there's only one thing they're thinking about."

As for Cummins' claims of having no knowledge of the plan to tamper with the ball?

"We have to believe it," Chappell said.

"Pat's a very honourable man and very talented on the field, but I think he's very talented off the field as well.

"I think from a cricket point of view they just need to move on and focus on what's in front of them."

Khawaja was due to make an appearance at a book-signing event in Merrylands on Saturday, but publishers Pelican said it unfortunately had to be postponed.

Washington: At the end of the film Love Actually, the split screen gradually expands to show hundreds of different scenes from airports: people hugging, crying, saying their hellos or goodbyes. It serves as a touching reminder that everyone has a story; we all matter to somebody. It was somewhat the opposite at airports across the United States on Friday afternoon – hundreds of thousands of people clutching phones, hastily revising plans, corralling bored children, waiting in line to rebook flights, searching for luggage, queueing at Starbucks or the airport bar. The long wait for flights at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. AP US airspace handles about 45,000 flights a day, through some of the world’s busiest airports: Chicago’s O’Hare, Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson, Texas’ Dallas-Fort Worth. It’s rarely glamorous, but when the system works, it is pretty impressive. When it fails, it’s miserable. Such was the case when the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered an exceedingly rare nationwide ground stop after technical problems plagued critical air traffic control systems. About 15,000 flights were either cancelled or delayed, affecting millions of passengers and their families.

At Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, 31-year-old Madeline DeMaske was hoping to head home to Denver, Colorado after a whirlwind work trip to the nation’s capital. “Now I get one more day in DC,” she said. “Hopefully only one more day.” DeMaske was already on board her plane, about to start taxiing, when the pilot and gate agent entered to tell passengers they were stuck on the tarmac. She waited at the terminal for hours, hearing rumours that things might change soon. “My flight was cancelled five minutes before [the flight ban] was lifted.” Madeline DeMaske, 31, was already on her flight home to Denver when the ground stop was ordered. Michael Koziol Some gates inside the terminal were quiet, DeMaske said, but others were “very chaotic”, with long lines at the information desk. At the end, Jensen Huang looked broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted. After weeks spent denying allegations of infidelity and fighting to remain in his job as Nvidia’s chief executive officer, his surrender was unconditional. Huang’s usual take-charge demeanour had evaporated, according to a person familiar with the situation, and he’d started using phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care”. During the decades he spent building Nvidia into a multitrillion-dollar AI chip behemoth, Huang was famous for his attention to the tiniest of details, from chip architecture to the compensation packages of even the most junior employees at the company. Now, in the eyes of the people in the room, he had given up. The downfall of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang has been swift and unexpected. Marija Ercegovac It was a stunningly quick fall for a billionaire and tech titan who two weeks ago was the face of artificial intelligence around the world. With his directness and vigour, he had charmed US President Donald Trump, shaped global tech policy and drawn adoring crowds on his papal-style international tours. It’s hard to imagine the current AI boom happening without Huang, his company and its chips, and it’s hard to imagine what it will look like after his fall. As Harvey Jones, chair of the company’s board of directors, wrote in an email to employees after Huang’s ouster, “Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world.”

Advertisement

Huang couldn’t be reached for comment. Related Article Analysis

AI Jensen Huang once told me his two golden rules. He may have broken one of them When the news broke in late October that Huang had close ties with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, it looked like he would prevail. The board of directors, dominated by longtime investors, business partners and friends of Huang’s, was reluctant to act on the news stories, or even publicly comment on them. Most of the news coverage tiptoed around the exact nature of the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected spy. Huang denied to friends and colleagues that he had been unfaithful to his wife. He’d been denying it when questioned internally since late 2025. In one of his last interviews as CEO, Huang told Bloomberg News that his relationship with Alice Huang was typical of those with Chinese customers and executives. “It was all completely normal and not unusual,” he said. A turning point came last Friday, November 6, when a Financial Times story cited US officials saying that the relationship had been a romantic one. Soon afterwards, Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter went to Huang’s house to confront him, and Huang confessed. At that point, most of the board still didn’t want to take a public stance, but Teter, who is secretary of the board, told them they had to act. The board announced they would investigate the allegations. A prominent law firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, would lead the inquiry. On Sunday, Huang emailed the entire company, admitting to the affair, apologising to his family and vowing to “cooperate fully” with the board’s investigation.

Advertisement

As the scandal ballooned, there was evidence that it was, perhaps unsurprisingly, drawing Huang’s attention away from his extensive duties at the company. As part of Nvidia’s idiosyncratic org chart, Huang had about 60 executives at the company who reported to him, a small army by normal management standards. The whole company had to file emails with their top five priorities, which Huang used to check that everyone was working on what he considered most important. Normally he responded to them immediately at all hours of the day and night. In recent days, the response times had grown longer. The Nvidia board acted fast after a reported that Huang was having an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Huang was also having an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. This time, the board acted quickly. Directors assembled remotely on Wednesday, and the meeting lasted late into the night. In the end, Huang was given no choice but to resign, ending his association with the company completely. The next morning, the board announced that chief financial officer Colette Kress would step in as interim CEO. She was quick to try to reassure rattled employees. “I believe deeply in this company and in its future,” Kress wrote in an email reviewed by Bloomberg. “More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy. The board, staff and I recognise that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you.” She pledged to hold an all-hands meeting on November 18. A day earlier, Nvidia is due to report results and disclose what Wall Street analysts predict will be a near doubling of quarterly sales growth.

Advertisement

Now, the board confronts the difficult challenge of finding a replacement for Huang. Some executives considered likely to end up on the shortlist: Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su and Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas. It’s hard to imagine anyone filling all Huang’s roles – technologist, executive, marketer, lobbyist, mascot – and the company never bothered to create a traditional succession plan. For better or worse, Nvidia will begin to look more like a regular company, managed in a more regular way. Related Article AI The rise and fall of leather jacket-clad tech ‘godfather’ Jensen Huang As for Huang himself, he won’t be able to retreat from public life, even if he wants to. In the coming weeks he’s expected to testify before Congress, where politicians will ask him about his relationship with Alice Huang and whether it might have put some of the secrets of Nvidia’s state-of-the-art chips at risk. According to people who’ve spoken with him in recent days, Huang has already taken a penitent turn, castigating himself as a “piece of shit” . He claims he does not care what happens to him at this point. His main concern, he says, is his wife, and not “ruining the lives” of the multiple women now romantically linked to him in the public imagination. Ingrid Stitt’s department repeatedly warned her about the CFMEU’s conduct. Ruby Alexander Jenkin described regular high-level meetings with then-minister Ingrid Stitt and her staff as one of the ways WorkSafe communicated the CFMEU’s disruption of major projects using unfounded safety claims – particularly on the West Gate Tunnel, which was beset by delays and cost blowouts. “These issues were recorded within WorkSafe in weekly email updates and highlighted in written and oral briefings to the minister’s office, including by the CEO personally,” he said.

David Warner appeared on a Kayo Sports panel on Friday. The former opener has thrown his weight behind friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja. Instagram “It looks like they had decided who they wanted to blame from the very beginning, ran a shoddy investigation to serve the purpose, and now they want to maintain the false narrative that the bowlers had no idea. That stinks of a cover-up.” This masthead has reached out to representatives of Hazlewood, Starc and Lyon for comment. Cricket Australia released a statement in response to Warner’s allegation, saying the organisation respected the differing recollections among the 2018 playing group.

The statement did not say if any of the three players were interviewed by investigator Iain Roy. “As we have stated previously, all players were given the opportunity to speak at the time of the initial investigation [into the ball-tampering saga] and have had the ability to come forward with new evidence in the eight years since,” a CA spokesman said. “Subsequently, CA has respected every player and former players’ right to provide their own version of events.” Loading CA chief Todd Greenberg said this week the governing body would not be reopening the investigation, despite Khawaja’s allegations.

title: Inside the south-west Sydney Labor branch threatening to topple a sitting MP

NSW Labor is considering rolling a sitting minister while also blocking the ascension of his main local rival, part of an increasingly messy preselection poisoned by months of bitter infighting and accusations of branch stacking in their south-west Sydney seat. This masthead revealed on Thursday that NSW Fair Trade Minister Anoulack Chanthivong is facing a revolt from local branches in his electorate of Macquarie Fields. Despite it being widely known that he would lose a rank-and-file ballot, neither Premier Chris Minns nor party head office have intervened. His main rival is Masood Chowdhury, the deputy mayor of Campbelltown Council and the president of the largest branch in the electorate. Campbelltown Deputy Mayor Masood Chowdhury (left) is pushing to win preselection against sitting MP Anoulack Chanthivong. Facebook/Sitthixay Ditthavong There is a growing unwillingness to save Chanthivong via a referral to the party’s national executive. The MP has endured a torrid term as a minister and has alienated key stakeholders, including the union movement, as both fair trading and corrections minister. Even if he survives preselection, Chanthivong will not be a minister if the Minns government is re-elected in March.

Advertisement

The reluctance to save Chanthivong stands in sharp contrast to a series of “captain’s calls” made by Minns to install candidates in seats such as Winston Hills, Wallsend and Wyong. However, there is also no appetite to open the door for Chowdhury to enter parliament. The party finds itself in a difficult position in the seat. Installing a third candidate via national executive referral would be a break with the convention of not rolling sitting ministers, and risk angering locals keen to back Chowdhury. His branch — Ingleburn-Macquarie Fields — has faced multiple complaints of stacking from Chanthivong and branch members amid a surge in discounted membership numbers, a senior party source said. But, the same source said, the minister had failed to provide the party with sufficient evidence to warrant the same kind of intervention head office has made in other areas recently. A membership list for Chowdhury’s branch obtained by this masthead reveals a surge in new members joining over the past two years, fuelling allegations from branch members he has stacked the group with his own supporters to win preselection for the safe Labor seat.

Advertisement

The list shows the Ingleburn-Macquarie Fields branch of NSW Labor had 152 members in its more than 30 years of operation. But in the past five years, 149 members have signed up, including 86 in the past two years alone. The majority of the new members are listed as “concessional”, meaning they are required to pay a significantly discounted rate to be part of the branch. (There is no evidence to suggest Chowdhury recruited the members.) Related Article Exclusive

NSW Votes The premier made captain’s calls in crucial seats. He hasn’t saved this minister Branch stacking – recruiting party members to a specific branch to change an outcome, such as a preselection vote – is not illegal and never clear-cut: one member’s accusation of filling a branch with cronies to support a vote is another member’s active community engagement. “There’s no stacking,” Chowdhury said on Friday. He said his branch never exceeded the party-mandated cap of five new members per meeting, and that the party had investigated his branch “one and a half years ago”, but “they couldn’t find anything”. “South Asians love politics,” he said. “It’s not my family connections. They’re different people, different communities, different colours. It’s very tidy.” Earlier in the week, he told this masthead: “I’m definitely interested to run. I’m telling you honestly, I’m going to win the preselection.”

Advertisement

Longtime branch members believed stacking began in the years after NSW emerged from COVID restrictions. The branch had booked a small room at the Ingleburn RSL for a meeting, expecting a few dozen attendees. More than 100 people showed up, identifying themselves as members and voting as a bloc supporting Chowdhury. Mike Freelander, the federal MP for Macarthur, had attended the branch’s meetings until they got too chaotic. He said the situation at the branch meant it was unlikely Chanthivong, whom he described as “a longtime friend of mine”, would win preselection. “That is a huge difficulty for him and I hope that the premier will support him, but I’m not sure what is going on,” he said. “Anoulack’s a good representative of our community, and he’d get community and electorate support, but the branch is controlled by a group that I have very little insight into.” But a senior Labor source speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss an internal matter said while Chanthivong, on the verge of the end of his political career, had repeatedly alleged stacking was occurring in the branch, he had failed to provide evidence to warrant an intervention. Masood Chowdhury (left) is presented with an award at a “Civic Felicitation Ceremony” after winning the vote for deputy mayor at Campbelltown Council in September 2026. Facebook/Masood Chowdhury

Advertisement

The same source, who was familiar with the issue, said that in October 2023 the party’s powerful administration committee directed head office to take possession of the branch’s books. A member of head office had attended several branch meetings, and new members had been audited for several months. Around that time, Chanthivong was provided advice in a meeting with Labor officials about the type of evidence required to prompt an intervention. That evidence never surfaced. Chowdhury has been a member of Labor for decades and has served on Campbelltown council since 2016. He holds significant influence over south-western Sydney’s Bangladeshi community, and leads several community organisations. In September, he attended a “Civic Felicitation Ceremony” for himself after being elected deputy mayor, at which 18 community members and leaders spoke and one presented him with an award on behalf of the “citizens of Campbelltown”. Chanthivong declined to comment. In a statement, a spokesperson for NSW Labor said: “Over the past five years, NSW Labor has significantly strengthened its anti-branch-stacking rules and has taken decisive action in areas where branch stacking has been established. “If there are any new allegations or evidence of branch stacking within this branch, they should be referred to the party via the appropriate process.

Advertisement

“The improper disclosure of party membership lists, including personal information, is a breach of the party’s rules and code of conduct. The party officers will consider what further action is required.”

title: The science behind Anthony Albanese's unusual hot mic moment
text:
In brief Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen were overheard discussing claims about the impact of phones on health.

Researchers have examined the effects of electromagnetic radiation on human organs.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese was caught on a hot mic joking with Energy Minister Chris Bowen about phone radiation and penises at the COP31 climate summit.

The prime minister was recorded speaking to Bowen on Friday evening as they waited for a roundtable discussion to begin in Antalya, Türkiye.

"Do you keep your phone here? Don't," Albanese cautioned Bowen, gesturing to his left breast pocket, sparking an exchange about the potential impact of mobile phones on the body, including the heart's rhythm.

"I'm more conscious ... I've stopped putting it in my pants pocket," Bowen began before Albanese interrupted.

"Because of your d--k," the prime minister said.
