Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"It's rather important — arguably more important than the heart," Bowen replied as the pair laughed.

Channel Seven initially broadcast a clip of their private banter on Friday evening.

A spokesperson for Albanese downplayed the leaked moment, saying the pair "were having a joke in between meetings," according to Nine newspapers.

However, the joking exchange raises questions about the impact of mobile phones on health, including common concerns they can cause cancer.

Can phones affect your organs and health?

A large number of studies have investigated these links, with some studies raising concerns and others finding little convincing evidence of harm.

The current available research does not indicate using a mobile phone is associated with harmful health effects, according to the Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency (ARPANSA).

Mobile phones emit radiofrequency electromagnetic fields (EMF), a form of non-ionising radiation.

Unlike ionising radiation, such as X-rays, this type of radiation does not have enough energy to directly damage DNA.

Research published in 2024 led by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) looked at data from over 250,000 mobile phone users and found use of mobile phones was not associated with risk of developing brain tumours.

However, there are some concerns about whether prolonged exposure could have other biological effects.

Some research has suggested possible links between mobile phone use and changes in testosterone levels, sperm motility and cardiac activity.

These findings have fuelled concerns, particularly around carrying phones close to the reproductive organs or heart.

But the evidence is far from conclusive.

Most studies examining electromagnetic radiation and its effects on human organs, including the heart, have found little evidence of a direct relationship.

However, one major UK longitudinal study found an association between longer weekly mobile phone use and an increased risk of cardiovascular disease.

The research found that sleep patterns, psychological distress and neuroticism accounted for between 2.25 and 11.5 per cent of the association.

Importantly, researchers suggested that the way people use their phones could be part of the problem.

READ MORE Facing fossil fuel criticism, Albanese urges world not to overlook Pacific climate plight

Late-night scrolling, disrupted sleep, constant notifications and the psychological stress of an endless stream of digital information can all affect the body's circadian rhythms, hormone regulation and metabolic health.

Poor sleep and chronic stress are already well-established risk factors for cardiovascular disease.

The researchers noted that these factors could help explain the relationship, although the study could not establish causation.

title: US resumes flights after air traffic problem sparks chaos
text:
In brief The ground stop was due to a communications issue affecting 22 regional air traffic control centres.

The US has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on.

The United States has lifted its order to ground all flights across the country after earlier communications problems at regional air traffic control centres.

The earlier notice from the Federal Aviation Administration said the ground stop was being imposed "due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety".

Planes already in the air were allowed to land, but those on the ground could not take off.

The FAA made clear there was no connection between the problem and the Microsoft outage that disrupted millions of users on Friday. While many are now able to access their Outlook and Teams, the issue is still being fixed.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the FAA was investigating a communications issue affecting the 22 regional air traffic control centres that direct planes en route between airports nationwide.

This was the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that the last time had been after the September 11 attacks.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication yet that "this was a nefarious attack against us. It's just a telecommunications outage."

"Everybody's safe. There's no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they're flying," Mullin said.

Second ground stop since 9/11

Mullin said investigators will look at whether there is any link to the FAA's nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system to help identify problems and reroute planes.

The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on since US Congress approved US$12.5 billion ($18 billion) for the project last year.

Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fibre optic lines and old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports across the country.

But Duffy said that another US$30 billion ($44 billion) will be needed to complete the work, which Congress has to approve.

The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the US northeast, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said, except this time on a nationwide scale. It may be linked to the outdated technology used by air traffic controllers.

"If you don't have that ability, whether it's because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you've got to stop airplanes on the ground," Arroyo, a former United Airlines pilot, said.

Saturday's halt was the second nationwide ground stop of all departures since the September 11 attacks. Source: AAP / Ethan Swope

"And not put them in the air where you're going to risk not being able to communicate with them."

The US National Weather Service also said on Saturday it was experiencing nationwide internet and communications issues. There was no immediate indication the two incidents were connected.

title: 20,000 complaints a minute. How was the Microsoft outage fixed?
text:
Key Points Microsoft said services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook, Copilot and other applications after the outage.

The disruption could result in over half a billion dollars in insurance claims, as billions more likely lost in productivity.

The Microsoft outage, which crippled popular services like Outlook and Teams, cost users over half a billion dollars, according to one expert.

Friday's outage lasted over 24 hours and prevented people from performing essential functions such as sending emails, managing calendars, and hosting virtual meetings.

Microsoft had over 450 million paid user licenses as of January 2026, according to its financial reporting, and over one billion devices connected to its services.

Disruptions and financial losses from the outage could result in numerous insurance claims, but the overall hit to insurers is expected to be limited, Mario De Cicco, vice president of European financial institutions at Morningstar DBRS told Reuters.

De Cicco estimated global insured losses from the incident at between US$300 million ($443 million) and US$500 million ($738 million).

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Downdetector logged more than 7.4 million reports worldwide, peaking at nearly 20,000 a minute, more than 1,500 times normal levels.

Microsoft also faced an outage with its 365 services in January this year and in October last year. Last month, it reported an outage of its Azure cloud platform that impacted its suite of productivity software and a range of industries worldwide.

READ MORE Microsoft says sorry for 24 hours-long global outage

Experts say the latest outage is a wake-up call for companies and users to have a backup plan for when services go offline.

How to prepare for future outages

RMIT Associate Professor of engineering Mark Gregory said companies in Australia have already been advised to plan for national telephone network outages after a series of failures.

"So if you're a Telstra customer, you need to have an Optus SIM card or something on another network as a backup," he told SBS News.

"If you're an Outlook or Microsoft user, you keep a Google or Gmail account as a backup so that you're still able to communicate or receive emails," Gregory said.

It's also important for companies, businesses, individuals and families to also have backups of software systems so that alternatives are available when one system fails, he adds.

He said businesses should also consider backups for human resource programs, billing, invoicing and accounting software.

"Unfortunately, I see many businesses that are not prepared to look at having that redundancy or backup approaches, and they simply rely upon everything being available," he said.

"And when it's not, their staff are really just being left in limbo."

Gregory said Australian businesses should have a mechanism to claim compensation, and the government should be able to fine big tech for outages that impact productivity.

"The loss of productivity will be in the tens of millions in Australia and tens of billions globally," he added.

What was the problem and how was it fixed?

Microsoft said the outage — one of the longest in Microsoft's history — was caused by server issues. The incident hit features tied to Exchange Online — mainly its cloud-based email and scheduling hub.

The company said a core process on the affected servers had become "overwhelmed". Once that happened, automated health checks within the system started shutting them down, tech expert Val Quinn told 7News on Saturday.

While the solution to the outage was to turn on the servers again, it wasn't that simple, Quinn added.

By the time the Microsoft engineers were ready to flip the switch on again, there was a huge reservoir of emails and messages queued up. Loading them all on in one go could create more problems, so they had to carry out the switch-on in stages, Quinn said.

Doug Jacobson, Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Iowa State University, said in a report on The Conversation that the pent-up messages were akin to a major highway crash.

Once the staged switch-on happens, email traffic does not instantly return to normal speed. Processing those long queues without overwhelming the newly restored servers takes time — typically hours to days.

Is the crisis over?

Microsoft said that services had fully recovered across Teams, Outlook, Copilot and other applications, ending the global outage that crippled online communications across businesses and governments for over 24 hours.

Dr Mohammad Goudarzi, from Monash University's Faculty of Information Technology, said engineers had been working to contain the outage's impact and restore services.

"Normally, in large-scale and interconnected systems, like Microsoft cloud platforms in this case, detecting a disruption may be quick, but identifying its underlying cause can take considerably longer," he told SBS News.

"These disruptions can also continue after access returns. Organisations may need to clear backlogs, check unfinished work and catch up on delayed decisions. Restoring the technology is only one part of restoring normal operations."

title: Dutch government collapse staved off, but crisis over tax policy continues
text:
In brief Coalition partner, the right-wing VVD party voted against the government's tax plan.

The chaos echoes similar difficulties inbBelgium, where the governing coalition is in disarray over budget talks.

Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten has staved off the imminent collapse of his minority government after marathon talks on Saturday.

The government however remained embroiled in a political crisis over tax policy.

Following more than seven hours of crisis talks with his coalition partners, during which the government's future hung by a thread, Jetten emerged to reveal they would stay together, for now.

"In recent days, many good things have happened, but also things that have not gone well... we have to do better," Jetten said.

"And that requires in-depth talks, which we began today. This conversation is not yet complete. For that reason, I will spend the next few days continuing these talks with the three coalition parties, in a calm and measured manner."

At 39, Jetten is the Netherlands’ youngest-ever prime minister.

The crisis erupted on Friday when one of Jetten's two coalition partners, the right-wing VVD party, voted against the government's own tax plan.

VVD leader Dilan Yesilgoz said she had been blindsided after Jetten and the other coalition partner, the centre-right CDA, had clinched support from left-wing parties to push through the tax deal.

"For us, the minority cabinet is a failed experiment and it cannot go on like this," she told reporters after the talks.

The spat raised the prospect of snap elections in the European Union's fifth-largest economy, just nine months after centrist Jetten swept to power.

His three-party grouping holds only 66 seats in the 150-member parliament, meaning they have to seek support from other parties to pass legislation.

Yesilgoz had called for a "fundamental reset" of the coalition and even Jetten acknowledged the need for a "serious fresh start".

Jetten called Yesilgoz and a top CDA official for crisis talks earlier Friday in a last-ditch effort to salvage his cabinet.

Coalition 'effectively dead'

The chaos in the Netherlands echoes similar difficulties in neighbouring Belgium, where the governing coalition is in disarray over budget talks. Both Jetten and Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever had skipped a crunch meeting of EU leaders in Dublin this week to focus on their domestic woes.

Polls show that in the Netherlands, the left-wing PRO party and their energetic young leader Jesse Klaver would win a snap election, with far-right firebrand Geert Wilders in second place.

"This coalition is effectively dead. We just have to wait for the funeral to take place," Wilders said.

Wilders had sparked elections in 2025 when he pulled his party out of government in a row over immigration.

Against the odds, Jetten pulled off a stunning election win last year, coming from behind to defeat Wilders by a wafer-thin number of votes.

Jetten won widespread praise for his campaign, pushing a positive message and showing that the far right could be defeated in Europe.

After four months of haggling with the CDA and VVD leaders to form a coalition, he was finally sworn in as prime minister in February, becoming the country's first openly gay leader.

title: The Microsoft outage is part of a growing trend. This is how to prepare for further disruption
text:
Today's Microsoft outage has highlighted the risks of relying on cloud-based communications and Australians should be expecting more disruptions in the future, one expert says.

RMIT Associate Professor of engineering Mark Gregory says companies are not applying best practice in their processes.

"If we look at the outages that have occurred with Optus and Telstra, and also Vodafone, in some way they've all related back to a reduction in the amount of funds being put into the engineering side of the business," he said.

"So that when equipment goes down, or it's misconfigured, you then end up with a catastrophic outcome."

A major Telstra mobile outage in July that sparked chaos, with Triple Zero calls and businesses affected, was linked to the failure to maintain ageing equipment.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Gregory said engineering processes developed over hundreds of years generally follow a path of testing, checking with small groups, small pilot platforms and testing again before changes are rolled out.

"But that process is often either not used, or it's shortened because of the timelines that companies place on their engineering teams."

The Microsoft outage on Friday disrupted the use of popular programs such as Outlook and impacted the Australian Federal Police and Australian Security Intelligence Organisation.

Microsoft reported a widespread outage on Friday that left users unable to access Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft services. Source: Getty / Scott Olson

Gregory said a network misconfiguration — when settings don't match what the network expects — appears to have resulted in some cloud servers being disconnected from Outlook.

"Unbelieveably, they've had to reboot them to get them to rejoin the cloud," Gregory said.

He said businesses are trying to speed up the process of making changes, updates or improvements to their software and systems, and this is coming at a cost.

"The updates have been coming very quickly nowadays compared with what we experienced 10 or 15 years ago."

These frequent updates, along with increasing hacking attacks, have seen a rise in outages in recent years, but there are actions businesses and individuals can take to minimise the disruption.

What can Australians do?

Gregory said companies in Australia have already been advised to plan for national outages of telephone networks after a series of failures.

"So if you're a Telstra customer, you need to have an Optus SIM card or something on another network as a backup."

It's also important for companies, businesses, individuals and families to also have backups of software systems so that alternatives are available when one system fails.

"If you're an Outlook or Microsoft user, you keep a Google or Gmail account as a backup so that you're still able to communicate or receive emails," Gregory said.

Software is increasingly connected to cloud servers and he said businesses should also consider backups for human resource progams, billing, invoicing and accounting software.

"Unfortunately, I see many businesses that are not prepared to look at having that redundancy or backup approaches, and they simply rely upon everything being available," he said.

"And when it's not, their staff are really just being left in limbo.

The worst possible outcome is where companies order staff to take leave, which some of them do.

"Therefore, the problem becomes one that the staff have to carry."

In the past, businesses stored data and software programs within their own systems and offices.

"Due to the cost of doing that, over time companies have migrated their email into the cloud to use Office 365 or other hosted solutions," he said.

But Gregory said businesses are starting to understand the importance of having greater control over their services.

Businesses are increasing relying on cloud services rather than storing data and systems on their own in-house servers. Source: Getty / Jetta Productions Inc

"If you have your systems and services being provided from a long way away, such as the United States or Asia, the chances of failure increase," he said.

"'[Locating] them locally — such as within their own business or within the cloud situated in Sydney or Melbourne or Brisbane — you do see less outages when that occurs."

The advantage of this approach could be seen during the Microsoft outage as businesses whose emails were hosted by a company separate to the Microsoft Exchange Online, were still able to use programs such as Outlook despite the wider disruption.

'Part of our daily lives'

SBS has previously spoken to experts who say it's time for individuals and businesses to stop putting so much data and other information online, but Gregory said the computerisation of business processes is probably not going to change.

"It's a typical part of our daily lives today," he said.

"The question for many organisations has to be whether they rely solely upon cloud solution providers, or do they utilise alternative approaches such as self-hosted [services] or having those software packages run within the organisation."

Gregory said organisations need to work out the best options for themselves so they can still operate when these incidents occur.

"The only downside of course is cost," he said.

"You're paying for this alternative solution. [But] it's very difficult for companies to have hundreds or thousands of staff sitting around looking at computers unable to do anything, it's not productive.

Gregory says organisations also need address hacking attacks, which are on the rise partly because AI is making them easier.

"Nearly every major organisation in Australia has been hacked," he said.

"Quite often it's been because of a reluctance by the management teams and those organisations to actually spend the money that's needed to protect the company from hackers."

He believes the fines for failing to adopt best practice approaches are very low, and so companies were still underspending.

"The next phase will be class actions and people suing companies for losing their personal data," he said.

"And we really need to see more of that because Australia is still being hacked too often."

title: Cricket's war of words ramps up as Warner claims Khawaja was thrown 'under the bus'
text:
In brief Sandpapergate reemerged this week after Usman Khawaja claimed the entire team knew about the 2018 ball-tampering plot.

Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins denied the allegations, prompting a rebuke from David Warner.

Former cricketer David Warner has accused Pat Cummins of throwing Usman Khawaja "under the bus" after the Australian cricket captain rejected claims that the whole team was aware of the 2018 ball-tampering plot.

During a 70-minute press conference on Friday morning, Cummins broke his silence about sandpapergate, saying Khawaja's version of events was "complete and utter nonsense".

The scandal resurfaced this week after Khawaja, who retired from international cricket in January, claimed in his new autobiography, Sabr, that the entire team knew about ball tampering during the third Test match against South Africa in Cape Town in 2018.

The allegations contradict the findings of a Cricket Australia investigation, which found Cameron Bancroft, who was filmed placing sandpaper down his cricket pants on the field, Steve Smith and Warner were the only ones involved in the ball-tampering, and it was a one-off incident.

The trio were subsequently suspended and fined.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Warner, who earlier this week said Khawaja's claims were "100 per cent accurate", on Friday defended Khawaja and hit back at Cummins.

"I still stick by Uzzie and what he's written in that book, because it is the truth, and I really, really support him," Warner said on Fox Cricket.

"I actually feel for him at the moment. I actually feel that today, the captain threw Uzzie under the bus, and I’m very, very disappointed about that.

"All three of us [Warner, Bancroft, Smith] have paid a big price in this thing. I hadn’t spoken about it in eight years, but at the end of the day, we’ve got to live with these consequences daily. We've been served a life punishment."

Warner stood by his claim that the Cricket Australia investigation had been mismanaged.

"The way it was handled in the first place, it was hard for us to go back and give more evidence. I feel like it was a botched investigation," he said.

"It was a quick one to get it over and done with. Some of the questions were quite challenging in the way it was being planted on us, and we had to move on and just accept responsibility, the three of us, and we ultimately did.

"We don't have that opportunity to go there and speak again. [Cricket Australia CEO] Todd Greenberg squashed that the other day. There probably are going to be conversations behind the scenes after this."

Warner later added he would one day tell his side of the story and he was "not going to accept until the truth is out there".

Cricket Australia has stood by its findings, with Greenberg saying on Tuesday it would not reopen the investigation.

Khawaja has faced criticism over the timing of his allegations, which coincide with the release of his book.

Cummins: 'Complete and utter nonsense'

Earlier on Friday, Cummins rejected Khawja's claims, saying: "When [Usman Khawaja] says we all knew, if by that he means that we knew sandpaper was going out in the field, he's 100 per cent wrong."

"I have said that consistently for the last eight years. I did not know that was happening, but I think Usman actually says things that are actually far more serious than that."

He also alleged there had been ball tampering during an earlier match.

Cummins said those claims were "complete and utter nonsense".

Cummins said Khawaja was a friend but "friends aren't casual with each other's lives and reputations".

"In his book, Uzzie's been casual with my life and the lives of many others, and I think Australian cricket. I support his right to tell his story 100 per cent," he said.

"I'm really glad that he feels like he can. But we have to be accountable for the things that we say and do."

Khawaja said in his book that he told Bancroft to be careful and avoid being scapegoated when the scandal unfolded.

"I was genuinely shocked this week when I found out that Usman admitted that he told Cam [Bancroft] to be careful when using sandpaper," he said.

"That's not the Usman that I know. It's not the Usman ... that has been part of a team that's helped rebuild this Australian cricket culture over the last eight years."

Cummins said the culture of the 2018 side was very different to the current team.

"At that stage I think [the side] had a win-at-all-costs mentality, had an ugly underbelly, and there were too many silos within the team," he said.

"Traits that I hope that everyone's seen, and I try very hard to eradicate for the last six years as captain."

Some claims 'probably defamatory'

Cummins said he had received advice some of the claims were "probably defamatory" but he would not be taking any legal action.

"You got to move on. It's been eight years," he said.

"You got to draw a line at some point."

Cummins said parts of Khawaja's allegations were likely true but other parts were "vague".

"Some of these things are probably true, and they are his accounts of what happened. But I think there's a few big leaps here where he's being vague and I think the details really matter in that difference," he said.

"Perhaps there was conversations with Cameron Bancroft around taking sandpaper out and how to do it. That doesn't mean that everyone in that dressing room knew what was going on.

"The way he's presented his story, I think he's done it in a very casual manner, and it affects a lot of people. That's what I'm grappling with at the moment because I don't think it's okay."

Cummins saw ball-tampering in Sheffield Shield match

Cummins said the only other time he saw illegal ball-tampering was during a Sheffield Shield match, when a senior batter, who he chose not to name, brought a bottle cap onto the pitch.

"It was dealt with. The umpires knew it as well. They caught him out and said, 'You've got to stop that right now.' It was dealt with. That's the only time I had seen something illegal out there," he said.

Cummins has also addressed footage published by The Australian newspaper on Thursday of what appeared to be a heated argument with his wife.

"We weren't having a spat. Becky was very frustrated, animated, and really not happy with Usman," he said.

"It's half very comical. Becky wears her heart on her sleeve. And half all a bit ridiculous, isn't it? We are here talking about something that was dealt with eight-and-a-half years ago.

"Now I'm walking my one-and-a-half-year-old daughter with nappies out the front and I got cameras chasing me and my family. For me, that's a bit ridiculous."

Others from the 2018 side have also issued denials.

Australian fast bowler Mitchell Starc, who in 2021 stated he had no knowledge of the ball-tampering, said on Tuesday his recollection had not changed.

Mitch Marsh, who was part of the 2018 side, refused to answer questions on Wednesday about the allegations.

"There has obviously been a lot of noise around this week and I respect that certain people have told their stories, but I’m not here to share mine today."

title: Microsoft services not 'fully returned to baseline' as recovery from outage continues
text:
In Brief Microsoft said it is working to resolve an outage impacting "users in any region".

Popular business platforms Outlook and Teams have been impacted.

Schools, businesses, courts, and government agencies are still being affected by a global Microsoft outage, as the tech giant says it is working to restore services.

The company said it is "seeing early stabilisation and capacity improvements" as recovery efforts continue.

"Recovery actions are ongoing and have progressed in phases across affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure.

"Global telemetry and customer reports show incremental improvement in several workloads; however, service health remains variable and capacity has not yet fully returned to baseline," Microsoft said at 9pm (AEDT) on Friday.

Earlier on Friday, the company had expressed optimism, saying it was "seeing positive results" in restarting impacted systems, but shortly afterwards removed that detail from its updates.

Microsoft said it has "no evidence of malicious activity" associated with the incident.

'A chain reaction'

Governments in the Australian Capital Territory, Tasmania and Western Australia said they were impacted by the outage. Service NSW said some transactions were unavailable and encouraged customers to delay their visit or complete transactions online where possible.

Courts in South Australia and Victoria acknowledged the outage impacted court operations.

The Northern Territory Department of Education said schools across the state experienced technical issues. Tertiary educational institutions were also impacted, with Charles Sturt University and Macquarie University telling staff and students it was also impacting multi-factor authentication.

Federal authorities were caught up in the scramble, with the Australian Federal Police (AFP) and Australian Security Intelligence Organisation (ASIO) confirming they were both impacted by the outage.

Microsoft Outlook, Exchange Online, Teams, OneDrive, Copilot, SharePoint Online, Defender XDR, Fabric, Graph, Intune, Planner, Purview, To Do, Power BI, Microsoft 365 Apps, Admin Center and Universal Print have all been impacted by the outage, according to Microsoft's Service Health Status site.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke told reporters on Friday morning that he had spoken with Lieutenant General Michelle McGuinness, the National Cyber Security Coordinator, and Jane Livesey, president of Microsoft Australia and New Zealand.

He said Microsoft believed it was dealing with "an update that has gone awry" similar to the CrowdStrike outage in July 2024.

"One thing we had with CrowdStrike was we also have a whole lot of downstream impacts where it was affecting the capability of a whole range of other products quite separate from that," Burke said.

Alex Potanin, associate professor in computer science at the Australian National University, said outages like this have significant flow-on effects.

"It's usually a chain reaction," he said.

"It wasn't just Outlook. It was also Teams and other parts of their overall server infrastructure."

While cloud systems can bring businesses more convenience and lower costs compared to hosting locally, a key provider suffering an outage can flow through to other interconnected systems.

How did the outage happen?

In the early hours of this morning, Microsoft first acknowledged it was investigating issues relating to Teams functionality for users in North America.

The next update from the company expanded the issue to "users in any region", noting reports of difficulties accessing email inboxes through their Outlook and Microsoft Exchange products.

The company said its infrastructure has been strained by "a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable".

"Our investigation has found that a core process on the affected servers is becoming overwhelmed, which causes the servers to stop responding and contributes to the capacity loss," it said.

So far, it has been attributed to an issue with the servers completing a health check.

READ MORE Why we're still living with password rules their creator regrets

Potanin said this is a normal check that servers run to monitor their status.

"For example, am I being able to connect to the other servers? Am I being able to use my memory without making mistakes? Am I actually still part of the network?"

When a server detects an issue, it will go offline and not contribute to overall system processing until it is fixed.

With some servers shutting down, Potanin said "many of the servers that they use started picking up a lot more slack and getting overloaded".

"But it may take them a few more hours before they come back online, as far as we can tell from the reports that they're posting."

Microsoft is sending updates through its status page and X account.

How have Australian businesses been affected?

The financial impact has already been massive, as the systems have been down since 5am AEDT, a privacy and security expert said.

The cost to Australia would be billions of dollars, said Ashwin Pal, of risk advisory firm RSM Australia.

"That's not just direct, but indirect costs as well," he said.

"But a protracted event like this can easily be the straw that breaks the camel's back for smaller entities."

He said his clients had activated business continuity and disaster recovery plans, but many businesses didn't have a fallback.

"They're just at a standstill — if you don't actually have a plan B, then you've got a problem."

title: 'Even a snail would agree': Greta Thunberg takes aim at Australia
text:
In Brief Greta Thunberg addressed a crowd at the UN climate summit in Türkiye on Thursday.

After not appearing at previous COP events, the activist said she returned to call for urgent action.

Environmental activist Greta Thunberg has slammed Australia's track record on climate action at COP31 talks in Türkiye, saying "even a snail would agree" that the country needs to move faster.

The 23-year-old's appearance alongside speakers from Australia, Nepal, Rwanda and Gaza caused traffic chaos inside the United Nations' climate summit in Antalya on Thursday, which also heard criticism of Australia's ongoing mining approvals.

Australia's Energy Minister Chris Bowen will lead negotiations at the annual event, which has drawn more than 92,000 attendees, and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese arrived on Wednesday for the leaders' summit portion of the event.

Asked whether she agreed with comments about Australia's slow record on climate action, Thunberg said her opinion was obvious.

"Even a snail would agree with that," she told the crowd.

"It's common sense. It doesn't get more clear than that."

Thunberg previously spoke at the event in 2018 and 2019 but criticised the COP26 event in 2021, describing it as "blah, blah, blah".

She returned this year to bring attention to the state of the climate, she said, and call for action to prevent further disasters.

"We are all here because we know that the climate crisis is already here and now, and it is already a matter of life and death," Thunberg said.

"And these disastrous trends we are seeing unfold all over the world are going to continue to exponentially get worse and worse.

"We have to start acting accordingly."

Indigenous woman Rikki Dank also spoke at the event, saying Albanese should listen to calls from Traditional Owners to stop approving new and extended fossil fuel projects.

Gundanji and Wakaya Traditional Owner Rikki Dank alongside Greta Thunberg at COP31. Source: AAP / Lukas Coch

"He needs to stop speaking and start listening to the Australian people when they say no more new coal, oil and gas," she said.

"He needs to stop speaking and start listening to our brothers and sisters across the world when they say they don't want us to export coal, oil or gas and the climate harms that they bring with them."

Albanese and Bowen have so far declined to address proposals to transition away from fossil fuels at the COP31 event, instead discussing electrification and renewable energy targets.

title: Nvidia CEO quits following affair allegations involving suspected spy
text:
In brief Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang is stepping down following allegations he had an affair with a suspected spy.

The departure could also have far-reaching consequences for US chip export policy.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang is stepping down, leaving the artificial intelligence industry without its biggest champion and clouding the future of the chip maker he built into an AI powerhouse.

Chief financial officer Colette Kress will take over as interim chief executive as ‌Nvidia looks for a permanent successor, the US company said on Thursday.

It named former Synopysys chief executive and board member Harvey Jones as its first-ever board chairman.

Huang, ‌who co-founded Nvidia and is its fourth-largest investor with a stake of about 3.61 per cent, will exit the board as well.

Nvidia shares in the US fell more than 14 per cent at the opening bell on Thursday, before recovering to a decline of about 5 per cent.

Suspected spy scandal

Pressure had been mounting on Huang in recent days after reports said the 63-year-old, who is married, had an affair with businesswoman Alice Huang, who US authorities suspect of spying for China.

Nvidia's board met on Wednesday to consider removing him, a person familiar with the matter said, after reports earlier in the day that Huang also had an extramarital affair with a senior company executive who reported to him.

Nvidia's chips dominate the data centres that train and run AI systems, placing it at the centre of both the US-China technology race and a massive wave of investment reshaping the US economy.

READ MORE Why Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's ties to Trump are back in the spotlight

The company also invests some of its billions in profits in other AI firms that in turn buy its chips, raising the stakes for the wider tech sector.

The departure could also have far-reaching consequences for US chip export policy, given Huang's push to preserve access to the Chinese market and his close ties with US President Donald Trump.

Revelations that US intelligence was investigating Alice Huang for facilitating shipments of Nvidia chips to Chinese firms set off a series of events.

Wall Street began raising questions about Nvidia's governance and Jensen Huang's personal conduct while the company's board launched an internal investigation and hired outside counsel.

US politicians also began to push for tighter curbs on chip exports to China.

Chinese authorities have denied the allegations.

Alice Huang is currently living in Beijing with the knowledge of security officials, Bloomberg ⁠News reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said in Beijing on Thursday that the US should stop making up "so-called spy stories" to justify technology blockades.

The leadership upheaval comes just days before investors are set to hear from Nvidia on its financial performance and outlook, with its quarterly ‌results due on November 17.

Earlier on Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang had also had an extramarital affair with a company executive who reported to him.

The relationship was with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of healthcare, the New York Times said, citing five people who worked at the company.

title: These Australians lost their jobs. Here's what they're facing now
text:
IN BRIEF More than 108,000 people were retrenched in July and August, according to the ABS.

Experts say AI can be both a help and a hindrance in job hunting.

For four years, Saskia Tjahja worked to help people with disabilities enjoy playing football — a job she "loved" because of the difference it made.

But in mid-September, it was all taken away. Her position was made redundant.

"It's been really tough because obviously I really loved working there and I loved what I do," the Perth-based marketing communications and events manager told SBS News.

"It was really difficult to say goodbye."

And now, two months after losing her job, she is facing an "anxiety-inducing" environment as "people are struggling to get jobs".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

While Tjahja's role was made redundant for reasons specific to her employer, she is among many Australians now looking for work amid a broader wave of job cuts across the economy. In recent months, redundancies have been most acute in banking and finance, technology and professional services.

The latest data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) shows that 108,300 people were retrenched in July and August; if September's numbers are similar, the quarterly retrenchment number will be the highest since August 2021.

The country's unemployment rate also climbed to 4.7 per cent in September, the highest level since October 2021, according to the ABS.

But the job-hunting process is not like it used to be — at least for Tjahja.

"I started immediately looking for jobs and applying for jobs. However, I've only been contacted once by a potential job opportunity, but I turned that down," she said.

Tjahja said that, with her previous experience, usually "it takes three months" for her to find a job, but this time she does not have "high expectations".

And in her job-hunting experience, she is not alone.

'Unsure about my future'

SEEK, an employment listings platform, also said its job ads rose slightly by about 0.6 per cent in September.

The number of applications for each job has been rising consistently and rose by 1.7 per cent in September.

Blair Chapman, SEEK chief economist, said the numbers mean "job seekers are facing greater competition for available roles, which can make the job hunting process more difficult", adding Australia’s "job market remains competitive".

Copywriter Erin Arnett has been navigating this tough job market for nearly a year.

She lost her job in January and has been applying for a handful of jobs each month since then, but she still hasn’t found one.

"It's been pretty hard, because previously when I've looked for work, I've been able to find something within two or three months, but it's been, well, all year, " Arnett said.

Erin Arnett is still searching for work, almost a year after being laid off from her last job. Credit: Supplied

"It's pretty disheartening not being able to find something and not being sure when you're going to find something.

"It's leaving me very unsure about my future, and I'm not entirely sure what my next move should be."

LinkedIn data shows almost 70 per cent of Australians believe finding a job has become harder over the past year. The platform's figures suggest that perception reflects a more competitive market, with the number of applicants per role nearly doubling since early 2022 while hiring rates in Australia have fallen by 21 per cent.

LinkedIn career expert Brendan Wong said two main factors are behind the tough job-hunting environment.

"I would say a challenging economy and the introduction of AI (artificial intelligence) are rapidly changing the face of work, and companies are having to respond," he told SBS News.

Recent ABS data also shows that, in the previous year, job seekers said their main difficulty in finding a job was that there were "too many applicants for available jobs".

AI applications

A higher number of applicants per job also complicates the process for employers.

Matthew Dickerson, Asia Pacific CEO of the global recruitment firm Hays, told SBS News this is partly related to AI, which helps candidates apply for "more jobs and customise their CVs at scale".

"As a result, working through that from an employer's perspective to find good [candidates] has become harder, because a lot more of the CVs look very good because AI has helped write those," he said.

"At the same time, the nature of the roles is changing slightly. And so employers are looking for newer skills ... For example, they're looking for people who've got demonstrable AI capability in the job.

READ MORE See the full list: The jobs Australian employers are struggling most to fill

According to LinkedIn, 77 per cent of recruiters say it's harder to find qualified talent than it was a year ago, up from 68 per cent the year before.

Dickerson said the growing use of AI in job applications has also made recruitment more time-consuming,

"They're having to actually do a lot more in-person screening with the potential employees to be able to find the people that best meet their requirements," he said

The human edge in a competitive job market

While AI is changing how employers assess candidates, Wong suggests a human touch could help candidates improve their chances in the country's job market.

"Relationships are pivotal to getting a foot in the door. It could be as simple as starting with the people that they know already," he said.

"Begin with a small interaction. It can be just sending out a message — reaching out to maybe have a coffee."

LinkedIn data shows that Australian applicants with an inside connection at a company are 4.5 times more likely to be hired than those without one.

Wong also cautions against relying too heavily on AI to write CVs and cover letters.

"The trick is to make sure that you're not just copying and pasting whatever the AI is coming up with, because everyone is starting to sound very similar," Wong said.

"Everyone is using the same kind of language, so to stand out, people really have to hone in on what makes them different."

Experts suggest looking into other industries might also help.

Chapman from SEEK said "there are still opportunities for job seekers across the labour market" and "in September, we saw growth in industries such as retail and consumer products and hospitality and tourism, while mining, resources and energy, engineering and construction recorded some of the strongest annual growth in job ads".

"It’s also worth looking at where hiring demand is strongest and considering opportunities beyond your immediate industry or previous experience."

title: House price falls haven't made homes more affordable, inquiry told, as banks grilled on profits
text:
IN BRIEF Westpac says construction lending has fallen 30 per cent, as high costs deter new housing projects.

Housing affordability has reportedly worsened despite falling prices, with prices forecast to drop until 2028.

The government's housing policy changes and interest rate rises have not led to more affordable homes or an increase in housing supply, but prices are tipped to continue falling until 2028, a parliamentary inquiry into Australia's four biggest banks heard on Thursday.

Westpac is lending to 30 per cent fewer housing construction projects than it did up to a year and a half ago, its chief told a parliamentary inquiry on Thursday.

The bank was careful not to pin the tailspin on the government's abolition of negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount in the federal budget in May, chalking it up mainly to cost pressures.

Labor's reforms included a carve-out letting investors negatively gear new builds — meant to incentivise construction investment — but Westpac chief executive Anthony Miller said Westpac was yet to see that take shape.

"There is some improvement in that area, but it has not come through as fast or as significant as perhaps we would like," Miller said.

He said governments still needed to work harder to spur new building investment, boost supply and improve housing affordability.

"Providing more resource for the demand side isn't going to solve the problem," he said.

The day before Thursday's hearings, it was revealed investor home loans had cratered by a record 30.6 per cent in the year to September.

READ MORE The type of homeowners on the rise as fewer Australians take out a mortgage

Labor hailed the crash as a win for first home-buyers because it showed speculators were retreating from the market much faster than owner-occupiers.

It also cheered an uptick in the volume of investor loans going to new builds, which jumped from 17 to 28 per cent between the March and September quarters.

Banks grilled over interest-rate profits

Inquiry chair Ed Husic said everyone in Australia seemed to be going through tough times, except for big businesses, with banks making close to $300,000 profit from the average owner-occupier 30-year home loan, a profit that is up $40,000 since interest rates began rising earlier this year.

"A big four bank is making a profit of $234 a week off an average Australian family with an average loan," the Labor MP said.

But ANZ Group CEO Nuno Matos disputed those numbers, saying banks are "performing their role in delivering to society" and "the mortgage business is one of the least profitable businesses in banking in Australia, and it has reduced profitability year after year, at least in the last 20 years".

"All Australians are feeling the pressures of the cost of living. That means inflation is high and interest rates are high, which is not improving the quality of lives of Australians," Matos said.

READ MORE See the full list: The suburbs where home prices have grown as much as 417 per cent

He said ANZ is not taking advantage of that, but merely "doing our job".

The bank expects home prices to fall about 13.5 per cent from peak to trough and stabilise in 2028.

He warned the economy is in a "dangerous situation" as governments and companies fight for capital to build artificial intelligence, defence capability, energy projects or deal with government budget deficits at the same time as interest rates start climbing.

"They are contributing to a competition for capital. We never saw this amount of spending in our lives, in our lifetimes," he said.

Liberal MP Simon Kennedy said housing has "actually become less affordable in the last 12 months, 5.4 per cent less according to the HIA (Housing Industry Association), despite housing [prices] going down 8 per cent, and then government spending at a 40-year high is adding to this interest rate pressure, which is making housing less affordable".

Westpac highlights supply constraints

Westpac said the government's policies had largely failed to boost home building.

While the bank's lending for new housing construction was higher this year than last year, Westpac says higher construction, labour, and material costs meant builders only constructed 5,300 apartments and townhouses this year, down from 8,000 last year — a 30 per cent decline.

"Higher construction costs are making affordable apartments and townhouses less attractive to build than higher-end dwellings," Miller said.

"The longer-term challenge remains supply — particularly the supply of affordable housing. Australia is simply not building enough housing to meet demand," Miller said.

He also urged the federal government to make a "break-glass decision" and fix the planning system and slow approval processes.

"It's an anchor on our growth. We will not meet our targets on housing or energy nor will we improve living standards unless we move faster," he said.

Meanwhile, mortgage arrears and hardship are rising among ANZ customers — with hardship hitting five in 1,000 customers, up about 10 per cent in six months — and arrears are expected to worsen before improving.

The bank reported loan applications fell 12 per cent over six months, with investor applications down 27 per cent and owner-occupier applications roughly flat.

— With additional reporting from the Australian Associated Press news agency.

title: See the full list: The suburbs where home prices have grown as much as 417 per cent
text:
In Brief Median sale prices have doubled from metropolitan Sydney and Darwin through to coastal cities and regional towns.

Suburbs along the east coast represent the largest growth in value for houses and units.

In 2011, Australia's property market was valued at around $4.2 trillion.

Fifteen years later, it's worth more than $12 trillion, according to the latest update from the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

But growth in property value has varied largely due to lifestyle factors and development booms, analysis by real estate advertiser REA Group on prices since 2011 shows.

In Pokolbin, in NSW's Hunter Valley region, the median house price in 2011 was $315,000. Now, it sits at $1,628,000, having risen 417 per cent.

Rounding out the top 10 behind Pokolbin, the suburbs with the largest growth in median sale prices for houses across the country are Jordan Springs (NSW), Palm Beach (NSW), Byron Bay (NSW), Mermaid Waters (QLD), Bellamack (NT), Boolaroo (NSW), Buddina (QLD), Miami (QLD) and Forde (ACT).

Use our interactive below to see the areas in each state that have experienced the highest growth in median sales prices over the last fifteen years.

How about units?

The east coast also leads the top suburbs for units.

The largest growth has been in Palm Beach (QLD), Bogangar (NSW), Tugun (QLD), Jindabyne (NSW), Miami (QLD), Reedy Creek (QLD), Mona Vale (NSW), Currumbin Waters (QLD), Double Bay (NSW) and Casuarina (NSW).

In the Gold Coast's Palm Beach, the median sale price for a unit is $1.2 million, an increase of 260 per cent from its value 15 years ago. Similar growth has been seen in suburbs along the Gold Coast.

The Northern Territory tended to record smaller price growth for units than for houses, with the top suburb increasing 26 per cent over the period.

READ MORE Buying a unit is cheaper than renting in this inner-city spot

Trends across the country

From metropolitan Sydney and Darwin to coastal cities and regional towns, median sale prices have doubled in dozens of suburbs over the last 15 years.

Megan Lieu, a senior economic analyst at REA Group, says several factors have driven this growth.

"One of the key factors has been the lower cash rates seen throughout 2012-2021," she told SBS News.

"Borrowing capacities increased, resulting in higher demand from buyers and significant growth in home prices."

The majority of suburbs in the top 10 are in NSW and Queensland.

Lifestyle factors have also been a major driver.

"Any beachside, coastal and tree-change suburbs saw strong growth in the past 15 years as well," Lieu said.

"With Australia's population ageing, many retirees or older Australians have also migrated to Queensland, in particular the Richmond–Tweed, Sunshine Coast and Gold Coast regions where lifestyle and community meet."

There has been strong interstate migration, with many residents from NSW and Victoria choosing to move to Queensland in particular.

For other suburbs, their recent development contributes to the growth, such as Jordan Springs, which was only officially registered in 2011.

In the Northern Territory, suburbs like Bellamack and Johnston have jumped much higher than the rest of the state, with 313 per cent and 260 per cent growth respectively. The next highest suburb grew in value by 69 per cent.

"With affordability becoming more challenged, many Australians have moved away from metro areas, where homes tend to cost more," Lieu said.

"This has driven strong population growth in regional areas and higher rates of growth in these areas compared to capital cities. Unsurprisingly, the majority of the top 10 growth suburbs nationally were located in regional areas."

title: Finnish president brings Albanese into embassy joke that's swept the world
text:
In brief Finland's Canberra embassy made an innocuous post on its Instagram page earlier this week announcing a one-day closure.

The mundane announcement took on a life of its own, receiving more than 11 million views.

An innocuous social media post by Finland's embassy in Canberra has become an unlikely viral meme, attracting millions of views and reaching the highest levels of government in both countries.

"I have confirmed to the Prime Minister of Australia Anthony Albanese that the Finnish Embassy in Canberra is open," Finnish President Alexander Stubb said in a selfie posted with Albanese at the COP31 climate summit in Türkiye on Thursday morning AEDT.

The president was referring to an announcement three days earlier by the Finnish embassy in Canberra that it would be closed on Tuesday for a team planning event.

Set to a jaunty piano tune and accompanied by a video of the northern lights, the post was simply a light-hearted public service announcement.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

But thanks to the unpredictable nature of social media algorithms, the seemingly mundane announcement took on a life of its own, attracting more than 11 million views on Instagram and hundreds of thousands of likes.

Social media users were quick to embrace the meme, flooding the comments section with tongue-in-cheek responses.

"Bad day to be a Finnish embassy in Canberra enthusiast," one said.

"Is everything ok? Call if you need me," said another.

Other Finnish embassies also joined in on the joke.

"For anyone affected by this closure, the Embassy of Finland in Prague will be open as usual tomorrow," the Czech Republic embassy said.

Finland's ambassador to Australia, Arto Haapea, said the embassy was taking the viral moment in its stride.

"We started the planning day quite normally. We went through what a successful year we had this year, all the visits and then how do we build on that for next year," he told ABC News breakfast on Thursday.

"Then people started getting messages like, hang on, there's something happening on Instagram and elsewhere."

He said the response had been overwhelmingly positive.

"Everybody was saying that Finland has never been this big in the news. The other thing, Canberra has never been this big on the market either; maybe it's a positive for everyone," he said.

The embassy followed up with a tongue-in-cheek ribbon-cutting ceremony on Wednesday to mark the reopening.

"After 24 harrowing hours, international expressions of grief and an unprecedented outpouring of solidarity, the Embassy of Finland in Canberra has officially reopened after its temporary closure on 10 November 2026," it said on social media.

Previous posts by the page had attracted fewer than 100 likes, but Haapea said the embassy was now attracting real-life visitors.

"Yesterday there was actually a fair bit of traffic outside the embassy, lots of people were coming to take pictures and we put some brochures outside to make sure we spread the Finnish propaganda at the same time. That was all good," he said.

It's not the first time Finland has found itself in the social media spotlight.

Last month, the country's state-owned tourism agency launched a viral campaign inviting 16 singles from around the world to Helsinki for what it billed as the "most epic dinner date".

Called Love at First Bite, the campaign aimed to bring strangers together over a candlelit dinner showcasing Finnish cuisine, with the possibility of finding love.

Washington: At the end of the film Love Actually, the split screen gradually expands to show hundreds of different scenes from airports: people hugging, crying, saying their hellos or goodbyes. It serves as a touching reminder that everyone has a story; we all matter to somebody. It was somewhat the opposite at airports across the United States on Friday afternoon – hundreds of thousands of people clutching phones, hastily revising plans, corralling bored children, waiting in line to rebook flights, searching for luggage, queueing at Starbucks or the airport bar. The long wait for flights at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. AP US airspace handles about 45,000 flights a day, through some of the world’s busiest airports: Chicago’s O’Hare, Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson, Texas’ Dallas-Fort Worth. It’s rarely glamorous, but when the system works, it is pretty impressive. When it fails, it’s miserable. Such was the case when the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered an exceedingly rare nationwide ground stop after technical problems plagued critical air traffic control systems. About 15,000 flights were either cancelled or delayed, affecting millions of passengers and their families.

At Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, 31-year-old Madeline DeMaske was hoping to head home to Denver, Colorado after a whirlwind work trip to the nation’s capital. “Now I get one more day in DC,” she said. “Hopefully only one more day.” DeMaske was already on board her plane, about to start taxiing, when the pilot and gate agent entered to tell passengers they were stuck on the tarmac. She waited at the terminal for hours, hearing rumours that things might change soon. “My flight was cancelled five minutes before [the flight ban] was lifted.” Madeline DeMaske, 31, was already on her flight home to Denver when the ground stop was ordered. At the end, Jensen Huang looked broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted. After weeks spent denying allegations of infidelity and fighting to remain in his job as Nvidia’s chief executive officer, his surrender was unconditional. Huang’s usual take-charge demeanour had evaporated, according to a person familiar with the situation, and he’d started using phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care”. During the decades he spent building Nvidia into a multitrillion-dollar AI chip behemoth, Huang was famous for his attention to the tiniest of details, from chip architecture to the compensation packages of even the most junior employees at the company. Now, in the eyes of the people in the room, he had given up. The downfall of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang has been swift and unexpected. Marija Ercegovac It was a stunningly quick fall for a billionaire and tech titan who two weeks ago was the face of artificial intelligence around the world. With his directness and vigour, he had charmed US President Donald Trump, shaped global tech policy and drawn adoring crowds on his papal-style international tours. It’s hard to imagine the current AI boom happening without Huang, his company and its chips, and it’s hard to imagine what it will look like after his fall. As Harvey Jones, chair of the company’s board of directors, wrote in an email to employees after Huang’s ouster, “Jensen’s contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world.”

Huang couldn’t be reached for comment. Related Article Analysis

AI Jensen Huang once told me his two golden rules. He may have broken one of them When the news broke in late October that Huang had close ties with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, it looked like he would prevail. The board of directors, dominated by longtime investors, business partners and friends of Huang’s, was reluctant to act on the news stories, or even publicly comment on them. Most of the news coverage tiptoed around the exact nature of the CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected spy. Huang denied to friends and colleagues that he had been unfaithful to his wife. He’d been denying it when questioned internally since late 2025. In one of his last interviews as CEO, Huang told Bloomberg News that his relationship with Alice Huang was typical of those with Chinese customers and executives. “It was all completely normal and not unusual,” he said. A turning point came last Friday, November 6, when a Financial Times story cited US officials saying that the relationship had been a romantic one. Soon afterwards, Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter went to Huang’s house to confront him, and Huang confessed. At that point, most of the board still didn’t want to take a public stance, but Teter, who is secretary of the board, told them they had to act. The board announced they would investigate the allegations. A prominent law firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, would lead the inquiry. On Sunday, Huang emailed the entire company, admitting to the affair, apologising to his family and vowing to “cooperate fully” with the board’s investigation.

Advertisement

As the scandal ballooned, there was evidence that it was, perhaps unsurprisingly, drawing Huang’s attention away from his extensive duties at the company. As part of Nvidia’s idiosyncratic org chart, Huang had about 60 executives at the company who reported to him, a small army by normal management standards. The whole company had to file emails with their top five priorities, which Huang used to check that everyone was working on what he considered most important. Normally he responded to them immediately at all hours of the day and night. In recent days, the response times had grown longer. The Nvidia board acted fast after a reported that Huang was having an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Huang was also having an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. This time, the board acted quickly. Directors assembled remotely on Wednesday, and the meeting lasted late into the night. In the end, Huang was given no choice but to resign, ending his association with the company completely. The next morning, the board announced that chief financial officer Colette Kress would step in as interim CEO. She was quick to try to reassure rattled employees. “I believe deeply in this company and in its future,” Kress wrote in an email reviewed by Bloomberg. “More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy. The board, staff and I recognise that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you.” She pledged to hold an all-hands meeting on November 18. A day earlier, Nvidia is due to report results and disclose what Wall Street analysts predict will be a near doubling of quarterly sales growth.

Advertisement

Now, the board confronts the difficult challenge of finding a replacement for Huang. Some executives considered likely to end up on the shortlist: Advanced Micro Devices CEO Lisa Su and Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas. It’s hard to imagine anyone filling all Huang’s roles – technologist, executive, marketer, lobbyist, mascot – and the company never bothered to create a traditional succession plan. For better or worse, Nvidia will begin to look more like a regular company, managed in a more regular way. Related Article AI The rise and fall of leather jacket-clad tech ‘godfather’ Jensen Huang As for Huang himself, he won’t be able to retreat from public life, even if he wants to. In the coming weeks he’s expected to testify before Congress, where politicians will ask him about his relationship with Alice Huang and whether it might have put some of the secrets of Nvidia’s state-of-the-art chips at risk. According to people who’ve spoken with him in recent days, Huang has already taken a penitent turn, castigating himself as a “piece of shit” . He claims he does not care what happens to him at this point. His main concern, he says, is his wife, and not “ruining the lives” of the multiple women now romantically linked to him in the public imagination. David Warner has accused Cricket Australia of a cover-up of the Sandpapergate ball-tampering scandal. David Warner appeared on a Kayo Sports panel on Friday. The former opener has thrown his weight behind friend and former teammate Usman Khawaja. AAP Warner made the claim early on Saturday afternoon, a day after he accused Test captain Pat Cummins of throwing Usman Khawaja under the bus after the release of his memoir, Sabr. “As far as I am aware, CA did not interview Josh Hazlewood, Mitchell Starc or Nathan Lyon in their 2018 investigation,” Warner posted to Instagram.

Warner hit out at Cummins on Friday, just hours after his former Test captain delivered an extraordinary 69-minute press conference denying any knowledge of the sandpaper plot. “Pat Cummins was very well-prepared this morning and I still stick by what Uzzy [Usman Khawaja] said, what he’s written in that book,” Warner told Fox Cricket. “That is the truth and I really, really support him [Khawaja]. NSW Labor is considering rolling a sitting minister while also blocking the ascension of his main local rival, part of an increasingly messy preselection poisoned by months of bitter infighting and accusations of branch stacking in their south-west Sydney seat. This masthead revealed on Thursday that NSW Fair Trade Minister Anoulack Chanthivong is facing a revolt from local branches in his electorate of Macquarie Fields. Despite it being widely known that he would lose a rank-and-file ballot, neither Premier Chris Minns nor party head office have intervened. His main rival is Masood Chowdhury, the deputy mayor of Campbelltown Council and the president of the largest branch in the electorate. Even if he survives preselection, Chanthivong will not be a minister if the Minns government is re-elected in March.

The reluctance to save Chanthivong stands in sharp contrast to a series of “captain’s calls” made by Minns to install candidates in seats such as Winston Hills, Wallsend and Wyong. Installing a third candidate via national executive referral would be a break with the convention of not rolling sitting ministers, and risk angering locals keen to back Chowdhury. His branch — Ingleburn-Macquarie Fields — has faced multiple complaints of stacking from Chanthivong and branch members amid a surge in discounted membership numbers, a senior party source said. But, the same source said, the minister had failed to provide the party with sufficient evidence to warrant the same kind of intervention head office has made in other areas recently. (There is no evidence to suggest Chowdhury recruited the members.) Related Article Exclusive

NSW Votes The premier made captain’s calls in crucial seats. He hasn’t saved this minister Branch stacking – recruiting party members to a specific branch to change an outcome, such as a preselection vote – is not illegal and never clear-cut: one member’s accusation of filling a branch with cronies to support a vote is another member’s active community engagement. “There’s no stacking,” Chowdhury said on Friday. He said his branch never exceeded the party-mandated cap of five new members per meeting, and that the party had investigated his branch “one and a half years ago”, but “they couldn’t find anything”. “South Asians love politics,” he said. “It’s not my family connections. They’re different people, different communities, different colours. It’s very tidy.” Earlier in the week, he told this masthead: “I’m definitely interested to run. I’m telling you honestly, I’m going to win the preselection.”

Advertisement

Longtime branch members believed stacking began in the years after NSW emerged from COVID restrictions. The branch had booked a small room at the Ingleburn RSL for a meeting, expecting a few dozen attendees. More than 100 people showed up, identifying themselves as members and voting as a bloc supporting Chowdhury. Mike Freelander, the federal MP for Macarthur, had attended the branch’s meetings until they got too chaotic. He said the situation at the branch meant it was unlikely Chanthivong, whom he described as “a longtime friend of mine”, would win preselection. “That is a huge difficulty for him and I hope that the premier will support him, but I’m not sure what is going on,” he said. “Anoulack’s a good representative of our community, and he’d get community and electorate support, but the branch is controlled by a group that I have very little insight into.” But a senior Labor source speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss an internal matter said while Chanthivong, on the verge of the end of his political career, had repeatedly alleged stacking was occurring in the branch, he had failed to provide evidence to warrant an intervention. Masood Chowdhury (left) is presented with an award at a “Civic Felicitation Ceremony” after winning the vote for deputy mayor at Campbelltown Council in September 2026. Facebook/Masood Chowdhury

Advertisement

The same source, who was familiar with the issue, said that in October 2023 the party’s powerful administration committee directed head office to take possession of the branch’s books. A member of head office had attended several branch meetings, and new members had been audited for several months. Around that time, Chanthivong was provided advice in a meeting with Labor officials about the type of evidence required to prompt an intervention. That evidence never surfaced. Chowdhury has been a member of Labor for decades and has served on Campbelltown council since 2016. He holds significant influence over south-western Sydney’s Bangladeshi community, and leads several community organisations. In September, he attended a “Civic Felicitation Ceremony” for himself after being elected deputy mayor, at which 18 community members and leaders spoke and one presented him with an award on behalf of the “citizens of Campbelltown”. Chanthivong declined to comment. In a statement, a spokesperson for NSW Labor said: “Over the past five years, NSW Labor has significantly strengthened its anti-branch-stacking rules and has taken decisive action in areas where branch stacking has been established. “If there are any new allegations or evidence of branch stacking within this branch, they should be referred to the party via the appropriate process.

Advertisement

“The improper disclosure of party membership lists, including personal information, is a breach of the party’s rules and code of conduct. The party officers will consider what further action is required.”

The ground stop caused widespread disruption across the US aviation network, with delays and cancellations likely to have knock-on effects throughout the day. US-bound flights from Australia can now depart after the halt was lifted. Grounded planes parked on the tarmac at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport in Texas. AP Before announcing that the system was progressively being restored, the FAA said “as en route facilities recover, flights will be allowed to depart” – with flights being released gradually as air traffic control centres recover. For travellers flying to the US from Australia, airports are monitoring the situation and advising passengers to check directly with their airlines. Qantas said that the US ground stop caused delays to a few Qantas flights. The airline is continuing to closely monitor the situation and recommends customers check their flights via the Qantas app. Qantas said it is also offering additional flexibility for customers who want to change flights that were departing to or from the US on November 13 or 14. Meanwhile, US airlines have warned passengers to expect ongoing disruptions. Travellers waiting at LaGuardia Airport in New York on Friday night (US time). AP

Delta said it is “safely resuming operations”. “While flights have started departing, it will take time to reset our operation, including the positioning of aircraft and crews,” the airline said in a statement. “We thank our customers for their understanding and our people for managing through this disruption.” United Airlines said it is also resuming operations: “While a significant number of Friday evening flights were cancelled, others are still expected to operate.” What has the White House said?

Homeland Security chief Markwayne Mullin said the ground stop had no link to this week’s Microsoft’s outage, which knocked global communication offline. US Transport Secretary Sean Duffy (left) and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin brief media at the White House. AP Mullin said the ground stop never posed any risk to any lives. “There was no flight at risk. FAA was able to handle it. We did it out of an abundance of caution,” he said. “We’re moving at an unprecedented pace as a whole of government to make sure that we are doing the public justice by making sure everybody is safe, which everybody is.” Mullin also denied the delay was related to cyberattacks or malicious activity.

Aviation US flights grounded as it happened: Departures to resume as FAA lifts ground directive after citing ‘extraordinary circumstances’; Homeland Security secretary denies cyberattack, Microsoft outage link When was the last time this happened? A nationwide ground stop of this scale is an extremely rare occurrence in American aviation history. It is understood to be only the third time such an order has been issued nationwide. The first occurred following the September 11 terrorist attacks in 2001, while the second happened in January 2023, after the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions (NOTAM) system suffered an outage.

The timing has raised questions. According to the Times′ report, the AI technology was first unveiled at Washington, DC airports two months ago on the same day a separate communications failure grounded hundreds of flights. That earlier outage was caused by a circuit failure after contractors accidentally cut through a back-up fibre line.

A local couple paid $896,000 for a North Melbourne townhouse, outbidding two other first home buyer couples for the keys to the split-level home. The two-bedroom residence at 2/60 Courtney Street is spread across three levels and features a garage room, a bathroom and an open-plan living room that flows seamlessly onto the terrace. The auction started with a bid of $770,000 as savvy buyers tried to get in under the $820,000 reserve. Independent auctioneer Jack Cooper accepted the bid but called for the next offer to be “somewhere in the 800,000s”. He was instead offered a bid of $2000, which he declined.

“I wanted a little higher given the guide,” he said to a silent crowd. As he started to count down, a second bidder offered $820,000, which soon escalated into a flurry of bids ranging from $1000 to $10,000 until the $851,000 mark, at which a third bidder entered the fray. Independent auctioneer Jack Cooper runs proceedings. Luis Enrique Ascui From there, the second and third bidder fought until the $896,000 mark, where the second bidder stopped. Jellis Craig Kensington lead agent Zach Sianos said the buyers were a local couple looking to upsize. The underbidders were another young first home buyer couple, who had dad bid on their behalf.

Sianos said properties in the first home buyer market were still selling despite the cash rate increases. “It’s just price-sensitive ... properties with sensible reserves are still performing well,” he said. “Properties under a million dollars have got some good momentum at the moment.” The property was one of 676 scheduled to go to auction in Melbourne this week.

Earlier, an Edwardian home in Surrey Hills, in Melbourne’s leafy east, sold for $200,000 above reserve, with a couple fighting off three other bidders to secure their city residence. The four-bedroom house at 14 Norris Street was listed with a reserve price of $2.06 million. Featuring coloured leadlight glass, an arched hallway and high ceilings, the home is close to schools and other amenities. Marshall White Boroondara lead agent Julian Papas said auction proceedings began with a vendor’s bid of $1.9 million, which was soon countered by a genuine bid of $1.92 million. From there, the first and second bidders – both owner-occupiers – battled in increments of $20,000 before breaking down in $10,000s. At the $2 million mark, a third bidder entered the auction, after which the bids went up in increments of $5000, until a final bidder won with an offer of $2.26 million.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
